MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORT IN MONTREAL "GAZETTE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. This morning's Montreal Gazette contains a story entitled "Canada to Buy Two Ferry Engines Here Despite Lower Bid by British Company." This article is inaccurate and unfair and is calculated to do harm to the Canadian company involved. There are two inaccuracies I should like to refer to, the first of which is as follows:
Opposition leader Drew rapped the government today for not awarding contracts to a British firm which had offered the lowest tenders for engines for two new Canadian ferries.
There is only one Canadian ferry involved. The second inaccuracy is to be found later on, and I quote:
The two ferries involved are one which will operate between Sydney, N.S. and Port aux Basques and the other will link Yarmouth, N.S. and Bar Harbor, Maine.
The Yarmouth-Bar Harbor, Maine, ferry is not involved in this transaction. The third statement which is calculated to do harm is as follows:
After describing the consultation with the C.N.R., the Minister of Transport said he thought that Fair-banks-Morse had "influenced" the ultimate decision.
The word "influenced" is in quotations which would indicate that I had used the word in relation to Fairbanks-Morse. The words I used are as follows, and I quote from Hansard which I obtained this morning:
I think the decision of defence production was influenced to some extent by the fact that the Canadian National Railways had had a great deal of experience with the Fairbanks-Morse engines in the operation of their ferry vessels. For that reason the contract went to the Canadian Fairbanks-Morse people.
Therefore it is fairly evident that at no time did I say nor is there anything in Hansard to indicate that Fairbanks-Morse had influenced the decision. As a matter of fact, Fairbanks-Morse had nothing to do with the decision taken.

I am in every way satisfied with the report which the premier did put out and I think the best way of answering the question is to read that report, which is very short. The following is the text of Premier Douglas's statement Thursday afternoon:
"This morning the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner met with the Saskatchewan cabinet for some two and one half hours. The main purpose of the meeting was to discuss Mr. Gardiner's letter of April 24 in which he asked the Saskatchewan government to submit a proposal as to what share of the cost they were prepared to assume in connection with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river development project. speechtext:
The industrial and technical service branches of the department will administer it. This vote is the first step we are taking to implement the recommendations of the Walsh report which is of such interest in Newfoundland. As I said last night, we were very anxious that the report be submitted before this session ended so that we could actually start this summer. As soon as the report was received by the government the Prime Minister set up an interdepartmental committee with representatives from the departments of finance, fisheries, labour, mines and technical surveys, public works, resources and development, and transport. Those officials reviewed the report and recommended a program which we can embark on this summer. The hon. member for St. John's West has studied the report, I know. Unfortunately, however, it is not as yet available for general distribution but the main recommendations at the conclusion of the report divided the responsibility amongst the three groups concerned, the provincial government, federal government and industry. Our interest is in the continuation and expansion of the work we have started to do over the last three years-experiments in fishing, more work in biological research and also in the technical end of handling fish, demonstration of new fishing techniques, and the 68108-332
Supply-Fisheries
first steps in building up central communities along the northeast coast in order to attract fishermen to those communities with better community facilities in the way of wharves and breakwaters, and assistance in the matter of new mechanical driers which are now being tried out along that coast. That is the program which we intend to launch this summer.
The Walsh report suggested that there should be a permanent standing committee in Newfoundland composed of representatives of the federal government, the provincial government and the industry to carry on this work. We feel that for this year at least, which is still an exploratory year, we should carry on with our present officials- that is, the interdepartmental committee of the federal departments concerned will continue their work. During the course of the year we will be able to see whether a permanent committee set up in Newfoundland would or would not be a better way of handling this program. The important thing, and I am quite sure the Newfoundland members will appreciate this, is that we did want to do something this year. a note "appropriation not required for 1953-54." I understand that results from some change made in the department with regard to fur seals. I should like to know why there is not going to be any vote.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext: This point was discussed last year. Under the Financial Administration Act, an appropriation was made for revolving funds for various departments. This is a fund which will revolve. It always seemed a little unfair to have the cost of this department's participation in this fur seal convention on the west coast included in the estimates. Nowhere in our estimates was there any item showing the actual net revenue which we derived from it. Last year our 20 per cent under the agreement with the United States, which results from the proceeds of fur sealing on the Pribilof islands, amounted to over $800,000. With the consent of the house that item was transferred to the Financial Administration Act in a revolving fund, so that item no longer appears as an expenditure under the fisheries department.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext: But the fur seals will be taken care of by the fisheries department just the same?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
I am glad to know that the request I have made for a good many years has been followed out, and that is you are going to have all the skins processed in one place, no matter where that place is. I notice that during 1952 the skins were all processed by one concern, so that there is going to be a uniform processing and a uniform type of skin instead of the type we have been receiving on the market for the last few years. Although these skins were all stamped the same, they were not the same price. The minister says we made $800,000 last year, but if the skins had been all processed at one place we would have made over a million dollars. Seven or eight years ago I made the statement in this house that more than a million dollars should be made every year from this source.
However, there is some difficulty in this industry now, and I should like to get some information from the department about it. It seems that the seal herd is not increasing. As a matter of fact, within the last couple of years research workers have found a tremendous mortality amongst the pups. It has been ascertained that the mortality rate almost equals 25 per cent of the pups. I hope that the fisheries department will co-operate with the United States in connection with research work to find out more about the seal herd. I notice that within the last two years they have commenced to brand and tag the herd, but as yet they have been unable to find out where any of these animals go after they leave the Pribilof islands or where they come from when they arrive at those islands. The important thing is to see if the seals can be protected when they are leaving the islands.
I believe there are a couple of other nations who are taking a big toll out of these animals in the different seas. I understand that negotiations are under way with Japan to see if that country will refrain from poaching as much as they have been in the past. I only raise these points because years ago the fisheries department neglected the seals and in 1944-45 only had about $160,000 of revenue from that source. As I say, if the industry is properly handled it should bring in a revenue of over a million dollars, that is unless the herd goes below a take-off of some 65,000 skins. I should like to draw

to the minister's attention that Japan is anxious to get back in on the treaty. According to the treaty 80 per cent of the take goes to the United States and 20 per cent to Canada. I want to ask the minister not to allow Japan back in, that is if we have to give up any of our 20 per cent, because this is a revenue upon which you can depend for years. Mistakes were made some years ago when Canada had the opportunity of buying the whole herd. We neglected that, and since that time the United States has made over $40 million of net profit after buying the herd. We are now receiving 20 per cent, but I would urge upon the department to investigate the mortality amongst the young pups and to give every protection to the herd while coming to or leaving the Pribilof islands.
Another thing I want to mention is that you should continue to get the skins processed in one place. In looking up what happened last year, I find that on last years' sales there was a difference of $56 on the skins that were processed otherwise than in the St. Louis market. Anyone who attended those sales can easily see the reason why the difference has occurred. Let me repeat again:	Be sure and take your skins from
the Pribilof field for processing in the one place, as long as they have a process equal to that of the Fouke Fur Company of St. Louis, Missouri.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext: The skins last year were all processed at the one place. Last year for the first time we were on the seas and the Aleutian islands on scientific research with the Americans. As to the seal population, it is reported now up to 5 million seals. Our scientific people and the Americans think that is about the limit of what those little barren islands can sustain. It takes a great many fish in the Bering sea to support 5 million seals. Our problem may now be overbreeding rather than lack of population. The fur seals are perhaps a class that might be included in the new north Pacific convention since they are under scientific study, they are under control with regard to killing, and they are being fully exploited.

speechtext: There is one thing I wish to mention. I should have done so a moment ago, but I guess I missed it. What I wanted to say was this. The name "mackerel" has been hard to get on the market as a canned food. But when it has been marketed under a new name, that of tuna chicken, it had wonderful success. The matter was brought before the federation this last year, and I am sure it will come before the Department of Fisheries. When this question comes before the Department of Fisheries I hope those who are making the regulations will permit people to can mackerel and put it under the name of "tuna chicken". If they do there will be a tremendous market created, because canned tuna has no comparison with canned mackerel. They could not get the word "mackerel" to take successfully as a canned fish. A true and correct description of the contents of the can, including the vernacular name, and in the case of fish the minimum weight in avoirdupois of the contents and in the case of shellfish the minimum weight in avoirdupois of the dry meat in the can, plainly printed in a conspicuous manner, and the name of the place where the same was packed.

Large tuna used to be called horse mackerel in the United States and they marketed horse mackerel as chicken of the sea, but nevertheless it is a tuna. speakeroldname: Hon. George Prudham (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I have a brief
statement that I should like to put on the record at this time. I am confining my remarks to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, reserving any comments that I have to make on the coal board and the coal mining industry in particular until that item is called. Judging from our experience of last year, I would suggest that we might save some time if hon. members would try to follow the same procedure.


I would like to make a brief statement reflecting both the importance of the mining and metallurgical industries in our country and the assistance given by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys in solving the many problems brought about by the growth of these industries.
A few weeks ago, I had the opportunity of attending the annual meeting of the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy which was held in Edmonton, which shares with other areas of the province of Alberta the distinction of playing such an important part in the development and growth of the mineral industry in Canada and in the industrial development which follows in its wake.
As this tremendous development continues to take place in the mining and metallurgical industries in Canada more and more requests are made upon the services available in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, ranging from mapping to geology, geography, geophysics, and to research and development work in ore dressing and metallurgy.
With some shortage and loss of technical staff experienced in latter years the services of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys are stretched to the limit in order to meet the increasing demands from both civilian and defence quarters,
A few weeks ago I distributed to all members of parliament a summary report recording the principal services rendered by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys in 1952. The principal object of this report is to make available advance information which might prove useful in the consideration of the department's estimates for the present fiscal year.
Incidentally we received no response from hon. members as to whether they appreciated this and would like to have it continued. It does not cost very much to produce this report which we have been putting out for the last three years. If hon. members find it useful we shall be glad to continue it, but otherwise I do not think we will put it out next year.
Possibly a brief reference to some of the highlights of this report would provide us with a picture of the assistance which the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys provides to the mining and metallurgical industries in Canada, and to the public generally. The department comprises five branches; the surveys and mapping branch, the geological survey of Canada, the mines branch, the dominion observatories, and the geographical branch. The department also is responsible for the international boundary

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
commission, the Canadian board on geographical names, the explosives division, and the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
The need for maps and charts for defence purposes received increased attention in 1952, and this requirement will continue throughout the present fiscal year. There is also an increasing demand based on the expanded development of Canada's natural resources, and for recreational and other purposes. Over 900,000 maps and charts were distributed during 1952, more than three times the number distributed in 1947 and 250,000 more than in 1951. A further increase is expected for 1953.
The provision of adequate map and chart coverage is a task that must be spread over many years, as even the production of a single map sheet requires a minimum of two years of co-ordinated effort from the time it is commenced until the time the final map is available. However, this work has been greatly facilitated in recent years through the use of modern methods and equipment.
In 1952 the geodetic, topographic and legal surveys necessitated the fielding of 83 survey parties. Approximately the same number of parties will be sent into the field in 1953.
Now, a word or two about geological activities. The primary function of the geological survey of Canada is to obtain information of the geology of Canada that will be of assistance in the search for and development of mineral deposits. The results of its investigations also provide a basis for soil surveys, for the appraisal and conservation of Canada's mineral resources generally, including water supplies, and for the solution of geological problems that frequently arise in construction projects.
The work of the geological survey of Canada, both field and research, is coordinated with that of the provinces who undertake geological work of their own, in order to avoid any duplication or misunderstanding. In 1952, 78 parties were sent in the field. Approximately the same number of parties will be fielded in 1953.
The largest field operation in the Northwest Territories in 1952 was in the district of Keewatin and was named "Operation Kee-watin". It was quite different from the normal type in that geological traversing was done by helicopter. In the barren lands of northern Canada the season for canoe travel is not more than two months, and the helicopter project was an attempt to use a method that would permit work for a season of normal length so as to increase output and
cut down costs per square mile of area examined.
The project was definitely successful. Although the work cost $3.80 a square mile, which is approximately the cost by normal methods the area mapped was 57,000 square miles compared with about 2,000 square miles for a single normal field party. In other words, it would have taken one party about 25 years to complete the work by usual methods. Another helicopter-supported survey is planned for 1954.
Laboratory research in the geological sciences is presently restricted, owing to lack of space, but we hope to remedy this situation. A new building is being designed to house the geological survey of Canada, and the estimates of the Department of Public Works include a token sum towards the planning and designing of this much needed addition to our government buildings.
An office of the geological survey is maintained in Calgary where more than 90,000 rock cuttings from oil and gas wells were prepared for study in 1952. These represent about 900,000 feet of drilling, much the greater part of it in western Canada and the remainder in Ontario.
In the Calgary office a study was made of subsurface formations in southeastern and southern Saskatchewan. A detailed study and the log of a well penetrating the entire sedimentary succession in southern Saskatchewan was completed. The results of this work, now ready for publication, provide information of value in correlating the Saskatchewan formation with those in Manitoba and Alberta, and in the Williston basin of the adjoining parts of United States, where important oil discoveries have been made.
From all parts of Canada, prospectors, mine operators, educational institutions, farmers, and others submitted more than 9,000 specimens of minerals, rocks, soils, et cetera. These were examined free of charge and reported upon as to their nature, uses, and possible commercial value. Prospectors searching for uranium ore submitted 3,155 samples for radiometric assays, the results of which were provided promptly and without charge, as were those on 92 determinations of the specific radioactive minerals contained in the samples. A total of 123,321 geological reports and maps was distributed in 1952.
The geological survey of Canada has contributed in a very substantial way to the development of our country's mineral resources, and it has been and still is acknowledged as the essential cog in this development.
5266	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
The activities of our mines branch are directly concerned with all phases of the mining and metal industry-from the processing of the ore or mineral to the production, forming and fabrication of the metal ingot. Laboratories are maintained, designed and equipped to deal with special problems arising in the field of preparation, beneficiation and utilization of the products of the Canadian mining and metal industries. They occupy a unique position in this field and are not duplicated anywhere in Canada. They have grown with the expanding mining and industrial economy.
The growth of Canada's manufacturing industry, as I have pointed out earlier in my remarks, has presented new problems in the use of metals. The demands of the armed services and industry and the development of atomic energy require materials of mineral origin capable of endurance under conditions undreamed of prior to the last war. These problems are being studied by our mines branch engineers and scientists.
A list of current projects would include: the design of flowsheets for several new base metal mills, the separation of cobalt and silver in the cobalt ores and concentrates, investigations on the recovery of elemental sulphur, the extraction of gold from complex ores; investigation of methods of handling and cooling hot slags from titanium ores; efforts to produce titanium metal at a low cost; investigation of problems of low-grade iron ores; research at producing purer metals such as chromium, lithium and others; survey of possible sources of rare earths and metals such as germanium, studies towards the prevention of metal corrosion, devising treatment methods for uranium ores, the development of Canadian sources of industrial minerals such as sands, clays, refractory products and asbestos, the study of industrial waters, the study of rock pressures in coal mines, the problem of coal and coke preparation, the designing and testing of a coal-fired gas turbine, research on the oil sands of Alberta, and applied and fundamental research in the field of the metallurgy of steel, magnesium, aluminum and other metals and their alloys; and this, Mr. Chairman, is only an abbreviated list of the projects being dealt with in our mines branch.
The dominion observatories comprise the dominion observatory in Ottawa with its five divisions of positional astronomy, stellar physics, terrestrial magnetism, seismology, and gravity, and the dominion astrophysical observatory in Victoria, British Columbia, which is devoted almost entirely to the study


of astrophysics. Also much time and effort is devoted to research in fundamental science.
Two astronomical cameras, of extreme speed and capable of photographing a large area of the sky at one time, were installed during August last at the recently established meteor observatories at Meanook and Newbrook, Alberta. These cameras are approximately fifty times as fast as the best previous equipment and are being used to photograph meteors in a co-operative program sponsored in part by the defence services of Canada and the United States. The basic purpose of this program is the measurement of the winds and the densities in the upper atmosphere between 25 and 75 miles above the earth's surface.
The Meanook, Alberta, magnetic observatory is the base station for the control of all ground and airborne magnetic surveys in western and northwestern Canada. Together with the corresponding station at Agincourt, Ontario, it has been selected as one of the network of eleven key magnetic observatories throughout the world for the international study of terrestrial magnetism.
The geographical branch of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is proving to be of great assistance to many departments and agencies of our government.
The main work of the branch is carried on in the division of Canadian geography. There is a small section dealing with foreign geography and this, together with drafting room, library, map library, and a clerical section, makes up the remainder of the branch.
Regional surveys deal with the physical, economic and social geography of a particular region as they affect such matters as agriculture, industry, transport and settlement. During 1952, such surveys were carried out in Cape Breton Island, southern Alberta, the Wager and Resolute bay areas of the Northwest Territories, and at various points in the Arctic.
On behalf of the civil defence organization of the Department of National Health and Welfare, intensive studies of urban geography were carried out in several localities in Canada.
Probably the most important project being carried out by the branch is the preparation of the new atlas of Canada. The work is being done on an interdepartmental basis, each department contributing its share of the basic data, which are then prepared for representation in the atlas. The section on the historical geography of Canada, prepared by the branch, in collaboration with the public archives, is completed and sections on transportation, fisheries and urban geography are well in hand.

Mr. Chairman, a tremendous activity is taking place in the development of our mineral resources and it is certainly not out of place that I would have taken some of the time of the house to give you this picture of our government's contribution to this development.
I do wish to take this opportunity to acknowledge and commend the high quality of the services rendered by officers of my department. Their contribution to Canadian mineral development has been an important factor in the broad program of national progress. As minister, I am proud of their high standards of skill and service. I am sure that pride in the splendid record of their accomplishment is shared by all members of this house. We certainly believe that more of this type of information should be made available to the people of Canada; and that is the main reason for putting this on the record this morning.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while
abbreviated, the review given this morning by the minister is nevertheless a complete one in that it gives a comprehensive bird's-eye view of the activities of the department.
I certainly join with the minister in the words he uttered during the latter part of his observations, when he paid a compliment to the officers of his department who have done a fine piece of work in giving the assistance which their skills have made it possible for them to contribute to the mineral development within this country.
Having said that, I should like to ask the minister a number of general questions. One of these I have had before the house on other occasions, and that is the need for co-operation between the officials in the minister's department and those in certain other departments. I shall deal particularly with the situation in my own province of Saskatchewan, because it applies to other provinces as well.
I believe the time has come for a policy of co-operation between the various departments of government so as to assure in the largest possible measure the development of our resources for the benefit of our country, and also for the assistance of the nations within NATO in forging the shield of freedom.
Today in this country we are in the position where, more than ever before, the eyes of the world are on Canada, particularly because of the fact that other nations have become have-not nations while Canada has available vast hidden mineral resources so necessary to the development of our defence, for the raising of standards everywhere in the world. The minister mentioned a number 68108-333
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys of radium ore samples that have been examined by his department. I am going to speak particularly of that subject, for we in Saskatchewan believe that the development taking place in the northern part of that province has never been equalled anywhere at any time. However, there are not available in northern Saskatchewan the facilities for the transportation of those vast resources.
This spring there will be a uranium rush into the Beaverlodge area, the like of which has never taken place anywhere before. I should like to learn from the minister what collaboration and co-operation there has been between his department and the Department of Defence Production, and what is being done to assure that transportation facilities shall be available for those resources. I would ask him to tell us the measure of assistance being given by the officials of his department to the Department of Defence Production so that the maximum amount possible of these resources will be fabricated within Canada.
Certainly these departments cannot be compartments closed off one from the other. I suggest once again that the national government, in co-operation with the provinces, should have a policy whereby these northern areas will be opened up, and that available transportation facilities will be provided.
In the uranium areas of Saskatchewan most of the transport up to the present time has been by air from Edmonton or by water during the open seasons, whereas there could be made readily available without very large expenditure highway transportation facilities from Lac la Ronge in Saskatchewan to Beaverlodge. Also the old survey of the C.P.R., made from the Lac la Ronge district north to Stanley, could be used and it would be of vital assistance. According to the information I have about 32,000 tons of freight went over the 300 mile water route from the end of the rail at Waterways, Alberta, last season, and already 45,000 tons of freight have been moved over it this season, and the above figures do not include any freight for the Gunnar gold mines.
I believe that the Department of Defence Production, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Department of National Defence should have a closer liaison than has been displayed up to the present time. I contend that one of the first things that would be done would be to provide for land transportation from the closest available and convenient places in northern Saskatchewan to this area. The highway that would be built and should be built to that end would also be available, should war ever come, as a defence highway in order to assure that the vast resources of uranium in that area should not be closed

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys off. A defence highway such as I suggest would provide accessibility and lower cost transportation than has heretofore existed. It would also lay the foundation for the necessary railroad facilities in that area, such as those being provided in Manitoba today to the Sherritt-Gordon plant at Lynn Lake. Not only would it assure transportation facilities at a reasonable cost today but it would also keep those resources in supply if war broke out. One of the greatest authorities in this country on that northern area is Dr. Mawdsley of the University of Saskatchewan. He was one of those who went into the area when others said there was nothing unusual in the potential mineral production of the area. Recently he was the authority for the statement that if ever war came a very few paratroopers, I think less than 200 he said, could destroy that potential uranium development in northern Saskatchewan, or rather render it unavailable, and destroy the possibility of that area being one of the main areas for the production of necessary atomic power.
I therefore wish to ask the minister what collaboration has taken place between himself and other members of the cabinet, and between the officials of his department, to the end that self-liquidating works such as I suggest can be proceeded with. I am particularly emphasizing production of uranium at the moment because that is one mineral, one commodity, that above everything else is necessary today.
The minister referred to titanium and there are also potential producing areas for that necessary resource. However, I particularly confine my remarks to the need for providing an assured potential supply of atomic munitions of war and also a potential supply of those things without which our standard of living and that of other parts of the world will not be elevated as we hope it will be if atomic energy is used as it should be. I would very much appreciate hearing from the minister in this connection, for this is a problem that affects Saskatchewan, and not only because of its physical location, since this potential uranium area within the next two or three years may well prove to be the second largest in the world. And it is, of course, of immense importance to our defence efforts.
Indeed, only recently I was in the United States and spoke in New York along with two other members of this house, ministers of the crown, who contributed to that series. One would almost think that the people of the United States for the first time had come to a realization that there is something north of the international boundary beyond quintuplets and mounted police. One would

almost think they had recently discovered a new world. Certainly the eyes of the world are on the mineral development of this country. It has within it possibilities of tremendous expansion; it has within it the development of our country and an increase in our population beyond anything that we can imagine today; it has within it the need for a declaration of a national policy that will assure that the maximum of these resources shall be developed and fabricated within our country.

My second reason for speaking is that a few days ago I met a cabinet minister in the corridor and had a brief discussion with him on the subject of coal. Despite the fact that he is in the cabinet and that in this country the matter of coal has been a pretty serious one for many years, the subject of a lot of discussion in this house, his opinion was that the coal miners were paid so much money and they were so unreasonable in their demands. He could not understand, for example, why they charge $22.50 a ton for coal in Newfoundland, which is just 90 miles across the gulf from Cape Breton. It was a brief exchange of words, and it was not with the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys but another cabinet minister. I asked him if he knew how much the man received for producing that ton of coal, but he did not know. It was certainly a long way from $22.50. The man who produced it would get about $1.10 a ton for that coal and the rest of the charges between the pithead and Newfoundland brought the price up to $22.50. I believe that is something which would bear investigation. This cabinet member did not understand that, despite all the discussion we have had in the house. I still got the impression from him that he thought the man who dug the coal sold it for the $22.50.

I know everyone wants to get away, but I am going to make a tew remarks at this time on the subject of the coal industry of Canada. The federal government has taken some responsibility for this industry. After many years of presenting briefs-

It would not facilitate us much because I would take up the same amount of time then. I may say what I have to say now so that the minister can analyse it and make a reply when the coal board estimate is being considered. I think we will get along faster if we deal with the matter now.
I said the government had taken some responsibility in the matter. They accepted this responsibility by the passage of the Dominion Coal Board Act, which was assented to on July 17, 1947. At that time this agency known as the dominion coal board was set up. The setting up of this body resulted from the report of the royal commission which probed the coal industry from coast to coast. In this act the board was given certain powers which are contained in sections 6 and 8 of the act. Section 6 reads as follows:
The board shall study, review and recommend to the minister from time to time such policies and measures as it considers necessary respecting the production, importation, distribution and use of coal in Canada.
Those powers are rather broad; in fact they seem to be all-inclusive so far as the industry is concerned. Now, section 8 sets out the duties of the board, and reads as follows:
The board shall:
(a)	administer, in accordance with regulations of the governor in council any subventions or subsidies relating to coal voted by parliament;
(b)	exercise and perform on behalf of the minister such powers, duties and functions of the minister relating to coal as the minister may require; and
(c)	exercise and perform any other powers, duties and functions conferred on or required to be performed by the board by or pursuant to any other act or order of the governor in council.
I have heard it stated many times by members of the union and industrialists that, so far as the coal board was concerned, it did not have any powers at all or that its powers were very restrictive. These two 68108-333J
J, 1953	52G3
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys sections which give the board its administrative functions are very clear, and I think they are very broad. I believe they could be used by the board in the regulation of the industry.
I do not think the board has been exercising its powers to the extent they should have been exercised, in view of the condition of the coal industry today from coast to coast.
In my own end of the country the industry has been going through a process of reorganization. They have been trying to mechanize these old mines and lower costs. The unions and the mine operators have been trying to negotiate a wage agreement since January of this year. A conciliation board is now sitting in an attempt to resolve the differences between the unions and the operators, but they are not making much progress. The big question, of course, is wages. The minister might say, what has this department to do with that? In my opinion the department and the coal board have a lot to do with it, because the act from which I have just quoted gives the coal board the authority to regulate markets, subventions, subsidies and so forth. I do not think the board has done very much about regulating markets.
One should remember that we are only producing, working at maximum capacity in this country, about 17 million tons of coal a year. On the other hand, we are importing about 27 million tons of coal from the United States. That is not so bad if you look at it from the point of view that industrialists who use coal have a right to import coal if they so desire. However, when it comes to a creature of the government, like the Canadian National Railways, importing large quantities of coal from the United States, and then you have the president of the Canadian National Railways stating that maritime coal cannot compete with United States coal, then something is wrong. In the railway committee recently I asked Mr. Gordon this question. Why should we insist that Canadian coal must compete with coal from the United States when no other commodity produced in Canada has to compete with a like product from the United States?
Take your automobile, for instance, and consider the tariffs and taxes you pay on it to protect the Canadian manufacturer. If you buy a car in Alberta, Saskatchewan or Nova Scotia, you are paying a tariff on your car to protect the manufacturers in central Canada. That is one example, and you can follow it through the whole economy of this country. Nothing produced in this country

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys competes with a like product from the United States.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: What about farm implements?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: The same thing applies.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: There is no tariff on them.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
There is plenty of tariff. Take a look at your excise taxes. I do not want to get into that argument with you because there are all kinds of tariffs on those products if you want to trace them down. At the moment, I am talking about the president of the Canadian National Railways, who manages a government-operated system that is subsidized by the taxpayers of Canada, taking the position in the railway committee that Canadian coal must compete with coal from the United States or Canadian coal can go out of the picture. That is not a decision for the president of the national railway to make; it is a decision for the board of transport commissioners to make. Why is maritime coal not competitive in the eastern portion of this country? I am going to tell you. In 1951, when Mr. Gordon was before the railway committee, he pointed out to us that the economic market for maritime coal went as far west as Coteau in Quebec. That is about fifty miles west of Montreal. But he said that in that area maritime coal was competitive with United States coal. In 1953, when he was before that committee and it was pointed out to him that the small coal operators in the maritimes were about in the position that the industry 'was going to close up, that delegations had been in to meet the government with a plea for some re-arrangement of their markets, Mr. Gordon took the position before the committee that he was not going to pay any more for maritime coal than he was paying for United States coal. He said that the economic market for maritime coal was not even as far west as Moncton. We wanted to find out why that change had come about in a matter of a couple of years. I found out why it came about. I found out that Mr. Gordon himself was responsible for that change.
In 1933 there was a mile mill rate arrived at on company service hauls from the maritimes at least to Montreal. That mile mill rate at that time was fixed at 31 mills. In 1938 that agreement was revised between the railways and the government, and the rate was fixed at 5 mills per ton mile. Some time in 1952, without any consultation with the government or with the coal board, Mr. Gordon stepped up that rate to 11 mills per ton mile and at the same time he was hauling


United States coal from Rouses Point into Moncton at the old rate of 5 mills per ton mile.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Can you beat that?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: By this action he displaced maritime coal or placed maritime coal at a disadvantage of over $2 a ton in the Moncton market. I was given at least some understanding that the matter was being discussed by the cabinet, that the coal board some two or three weeks ago were holding meetings in Montreal with railway officials, and that out of these negotiations would come some adjustment of that rate which I am discussing. However, to date there has not been any understanding. I have a dozen press clippings here. One indicates that the Minister of Transport thinks there will be some subvention adjustment. The next statement is to the effect that there is not going to be any adjustment. To date I have not been able to get any understanding as to whether the agreement which Mr. Gordon abrogated, without any consultation with any government officials, is going to be placed back where it was in order to retain the competitive position of maritime coal, at least as far west as Moncton. It is a serious question. When the minister is replying, I would suggest that he give us some understanding as to what has been done to restore the agreement that was abrogated by the Canadian National Railways with respect to a company service mill rate.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: And what is contemplated to be done.

speechtext:
This is not a grievance that I am conjuring up out of thin air myself. The minister of mines in the Nova Scotia government, Mr. McKinnon, has made some strong representations on the matter. He wired members of the railway committee when the committee was in session, and he asked us to have some understanding and some discussion with Mr. Gordon while the committee was in session. We did so, but we did not get much satisfaction on the question.
The figures that I am using are the figures which the minister of mines in Nova Scotia wired to the members of the committee, and I think they were Liberal members that he wired. They came to me and asked me if I would give them a hand in making the presentation before the committee. I therefore think that, before the house rises, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys should bring us up to date on what came out of those meetings in Montreal in an attempt to adjust those rates.

The second thing that I should like the coal board to do is this. I am holding the coal board responsible for marketing Canadian coal in Canada. That is their job. The authority is given to them in section 6 of chapter 57 of 1947. On three occasions and in three questions I tried to get information, through this house, as to who were the importers of United States coal in Canada, and I have not yet received that information. I received an evasive answer that it was not in the public interest to divulge the business of importers at the customs. I did not ask about that. I wanted to know the names of the firms in Canada which are importing United States coal. I wanted to know that because I am reasonably sure that some of the large operators in Canada are importers of United States coal. I did not get their names. I think it is up to the coal board to find out whether coal operators in this country are allowing the industry in Canada to die because they can make more money by importing United States coal. If that is the case, then the coal board should have the responsibility of correcting the situation. There is something wrong when there is a refusal to give the names of the companies that operate in that business in Canada.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I think so too.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I have a great deal of respect for Mr. Uren, the chairman of the coal board, and for the other members of the board. I hope there is not any agency behind the scene which nullifies their efforts to build a Canadian coal industry and to market that coal in Canada in so far as it is economically possible to do it. I hope there is nothing behind the scenes preventing them from developing a proper fuel policy in this country. I think the time has come when we must develop a proper fuel policy in this country. What I say is this. Take oil and market it wherever it is economically possible to do it. Take natural gas and do the same thing, where it is economically more advantageous to use it in certain areas than it is in others. But make the greatest use of coal possible in the areas where coal is more economic, and there are such areas. No one can tell me that piping natural gas about 3,000 miles from Alberta down into Quebec is going to turn out to be an economic proposition. But here is something that can happen. People can change over their heating plants and they may build on the assumption that they are going to heat their places by natural gas; but in a few years' time you may be short of natural gas in the area from which you are getting it-that is something that has happened all over Ontario- or something may go wrong with the pipe
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys line. You then have a building that is equipped to deal with no other type of fuel; hence you are placed at a great disadvantage.
I think that someone such as the coal board should give this proposition of piping natural gas down into the province of Quebec a serious looking over before it is finally decided on. If we strike the situation with which we were confronted during the last war, what will happen? Then, coal was more precious than gold. Gold mines were being closed down at that time, and people all over Canada were opening up gopher holes in order to get coal. The same thing can happen again.
I say that this business of a coal industry in this country is not receiving the attention that, in my opinion, it should receive. From the clippings I have I also note that United States interests at the present time are looking over sections of western Canada, having in mind the possibility of developing a coal industry there with United States capital. When the minister was talking, I was just thinking what a wonderful job the department is doing in making new discoveries,, carrying on all kinds of research, mapping' the country, and spending a great deal of' money in that way. Then when great deposits of base metals are found to assure the economy of this country as the leading part of the North American continent and a great contributor to the rest of the world in the future, after all of the work is done and all that money is spent the government on no occasion tries to retain any of those resources in the name of the Canadian people.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: It is hard to believe.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Let us develop some of it ourselves; let us hold on to it for posterity, or at least take a controlling interest in some of these great basic developments. The government is doing the work anyway. Most of the technical work is done by the government and why they do not retain some interest in it is beyond me. It is just handed over to United States interests or some other interest to develop and to take charge of our national economy.
Before he finishes his estimates I want the minister to tell me something about the coal board. When the coal board was set up five actual operators or people connected with the coal industry from the standpoint of management were appointed to the board, but there was also a representative of labour on the board, the late D. W. Morrison, who was president of the mine workers' union at the time. He passed away. Strong representations were made to the minister on the-

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys question of replacing that labour representative on the board with someone who represented the people who dig the coal. I was rather surprised and shocked to learn that instead of acceding to the wishes of the mine workers' union and others, including myself, another coal operator was appointed to the board. I do not like to see that, because I believe in that board. I believe it is an organization that, if given a free hand and properly taken care of, can do a great job for the coal industry. I do not think you are going to get the real perspective if it is overloaded with people from the management side. You are getting a one-sided picture. There should be at least one representative of the men who dig the coal and understand the other side of the question. I have no objection to the man you put on;
I know Owen Hartigan very well, but he is a coal operator.
The principle of having a labour representative on the board was established when the board was set up. Instead of getting the respect of the men and instead of getting them to look to the board for some guidance in the solution of the many problems with which they have to contend, you find the men beginning to say that the board is just an operators' protective association. We have not anybody on it to restore some confidence among the men themselves. At the earliest ^possible moment the minister should consider placing on that board a man who represents the viewpoint of the men who dig the coal.
I am not going to say any more on this subject. I could talk on it all day. I just put my finger on a couple of the sore spots that I should like the minister to cure. I refer particularly to a representative of labour on the board. What progress is the minister making with the Canadian National Railways in readjusting the freight rate on company service? An agreement existed on it up until 1951. It was abrogated by the Canadian National Railways. Is the minister making any progress in the matter of restoring that rate and adjusting the subventions so that maritime coal can at least retain the economic position it has had over the years in the Quebec market?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I should like all of those things with respect to Alberta coal also.

Mr. Chairman, before the luncheon recess we were considering this item having to do with mines and technical surveys. I am happy to follow the hon. member for Cape Breton South who has laboured for many years in the coal mines as well as occupying other responsible positions relating to the coal mining industry.
I rise to speak at this time because of the serious condition of the coal mining industry, particularly in the Crowsnest pass. I have in my hand a number of letters which I have received from coal miners' unions and other interested parties in the Crowsnest pass area whose complaint is that the coal mines are running on only half time. The first letter I have here is from a local miners' union in which the secretary has this to say:
As you are no doubt aware the mines in the Crowsnest pass are working very poorly.
He means poor time.
Bellevue has worked for the first four months in this year the wonderful total of 45 days.
If you figure that out it means that industry in that particular section has worked only 2J days a week. Things are becoming serious when that happens. I am not going to read all the letters I have received, but there is one from a man who unfortunately became in arrears with his income tax. He wanted to pay up and he made the proposition to the taxation authorities that he would pay so much a month. That was not agreeable to them as they contended he should pay more. He said he could not pay more because he was working only two or three days a week. All this means that we have a serious situation in the coal mining industry in that part of the country.
I am not going to be too hard on the minister and blame him for everything. He does not cause the sun to rise in the morning and the moon to shine at night; he is not omniscient. Things are as they are. I have never taken the position that the responsibility of the government is necessarily to find jobs for people. If that was their responsibility it would be better for them to put the whole country in the government service and then perhaps everyone would be more or less happy. I do not think that that is the function of government. But I do think that the function of government is to adopt such policies as will keep industry in a healthy state

and provide full employment to those who labour in industry.
Of course you have to go behind the scenes and consider government policy in respect of economics, which I am not going to do now. Just as long as the government pursues certain financial policies it becomes their responsibility to keep industry in a healthy state. If industry is in a healthy state we will not have unemployment problems. But an unemployment situation exists today and it is the responsibility of the government to solve this problem.
I should like to refer to the reports of the coal board. First I want to compliment the dominion coal board upon the job they are doing. In their own field I believe they are doing an excellent job. They cover many branches of the coal mining industry. I do not intend nor will I permit my remarks to be interpreted as casting any reflection upon the dominion coal board. But with all they have done, with all they may have proposed, we still have this problem of unemployment. Perhaps they consider it is not their concern, but that problem does exist in the coal mining industry of the Crowsnest pass area and I expect that what is true there is reasonably true of other parts of Canada.
Not long ago I asked that a return be brought down with respect to recommendations the coal board had made to the government. I made this inquiry because individuals in the Crowsnest pass area were interested to know what recommendations the coal board may have made to the government. I fancy they wanted to know what those recommendations were, and whether they had been carried out.
I received what I must say I considered a somewhat peculiar reply and, for the sake of brevity, I shall read only parts of it. I had asked for a copy of all recommendations of the dominion coal board during the years 1951 and 1952 to the dominion government, any provincial government, or to any other person or persons. This was the reply I got:
The dominion coal board was created by statute, the Dominion Coal Board Act, 11 George VI. chapter 57. The board was charged with the duty of studying, reviewing and recommending to the minister such policies or measures as it considered necessary respecting the production, importation, distribution and use of coal in Canada.
Then this paragraph:
The board, with some preliminary study, adopted some five objects toward a sound coal policy.
And then five headings are set out. I should like to read one or two of them, because I have a point to make here. This is No. 3:
Finding of steady and adequate markets for Canadian coal.
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
I do believe that when the minister replies he might tell us what steps have been taken during the last couple of years, not by way of surveying the situation, but in setting out any definite steps. What markets have been acquired for Canadian coal in the last couple of years?
And then the fourth paragraph is as follows:
Providing of reasonably full employment at fair wages for Canadian mine workers.
That is the one answer I should like to dwell upon, because certainly in the Crowsnest pass area there is anything but reasonably full employment. I am not going to make comments about the wages: that is something for the coal miners to discuss with their management. But certainly two and a half days a week is not in my opinion reasonably full employment.
Toward the end of the return there is a paragraph which, in a sense, is a bit amusing.
I shall just call it to the minister's attention. It says:
The board, by its terms of reference, does not report or recommend to the dominion government or any provincial government. Reports and recommendations are made to the minister only for such consideration and action as he may deem advisable.
I do not know if that paragraph is from the minister's pen, but I wonder whose eyes he thinks he is pulling the wool over. No; the board does not report to the government; it reports to the minister. Who does not know that? No one supposes that when a report is to be made they call a special cabinet meeting, and all sit around the table and say, "Now we have the report of the board." Certainly the report is made to the minister. So far as this is concerned, the minister is the government.
With all due respect I should say that the last paragraph is in these words:
Any of these reports or recommendations that have been adopted by the minister and acted upon are set out in the annual reports of the board.
I visualized that when the board made recommendations they were recorded on sheets of paper and placed before the minister so that he could analyse them. There could have been one every day, one every week or one each month. I am not concerned about how many there were. But I fancied that was the way the recommendations were made. I do not believe a government would be so loose in its administration as to have recommendations made by word of mouth; surely not. However, these reports were given with the return, and I had to be satisfied with them. Of course I had them in my library, anyway.

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
I should like to read one or two paragraphs from the reports, since they were given to me in the return. In the dominion coal board annual report for the year 1951-52, the latest available, I read from page 19 under the heading, "Movement of Western Coal to Ontario", the following from the middle of the paragraph:
It is unfortunate that under existing transportation costs, the Alberta and British Columbia coals have been unable to secure a larger market in Ontario. The coals shipped for domestic use have been fully satisfactory in the markets supplied, while there are installations where the industrial coal can be used without difficulty. The knowledge that Canadian industries are becoming more dependent upon imported coal, due to our inability to supply them with our own products, is not very encouraging.
Then it goes on to comment concerning the possibility of an emergency in the United States which would have the effect of speeding up production of coal in Canada. To read all this gives a rather gloomy picture, does it not? It indicates to me that the industry must be on the decline. And I would say, too, that this was a report given when industrial activity in Canada was perhaps greater than it ever was before.
Then, at page 24 of the report, under the section dealing with Alberta and the Crows-nest pass area of British Columbia, and making special reference to the assistance given to the movement of coal, I read this paragraph:
The tonnage of Alberta and B.C. Crowsnest pass coal moved to points in Ontario east of the head of the lakes was less than half of that of the previous fiscal year.
That, too, is a gloomy picture. To continue the quotation:
One reason for this lies in the increase in the freight rates noted above. Other factors were the general reduction in the sale of all domestic coals throughout the area, the loss by fire of one of the larger producers and shippers to this market and the fact that the coal from the strip mines was not eligible for assistance until October.
The tonnage shipped to points in Ontario up to the head of the lakes was also considerably lower. The over-all movement of coal for railway use to Manitoba and Ontario was almost equal to that of the last fiscal year.
I read those two paragraphs to indicate to hon. members, including the minister, that the coal mining industry in the Crowsnest pass area is on the decline. Now that should not be. There is no argument about that.
Well, Mr. Chairman, if I might refer to this little summary that the minister referred to this morning, as did the hon. member for Cape Breton South, I too think it is a very commendable little booklet. It is very similar to the report of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, a little blue book that comes out annually, but it is a condensation, and I think it is very handy.


If it is not too much of an expense I would like to see it continued.
On page 65 of the summary of activities of this department there is a paragraph about coal preparation investigations. I will just read the first sentence:
Investigations concerning the marketing of finer sizes of coal continued to receive special attention because of their importance to the coal Industry in western Canada.
When the minister replies I would like him to state what special attention it was given and what was the result of that special attention. The investigations in respect of the finer sizes of coal were investigations concerning the marketing of this coal, and after all we must have markets for the coal because if the coal cannot be sold the mines are going to close. There is no argument about that.
I come to the annual report of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys for the year ending March 31, 1952. Under the section dealing with the 'ueJe division on page 85 I read this:
The efforts of the division were concentrated chiefly on technical problems of the coal industry, in the belief that well planned and co-operative research can do much toward enabling the industry to maintain its markets in competition with oil and natural gas.
I underline the phrase "to maintain its markets". Now, since I have read these paragraphs from various reports in respect of the amount of attention that is supposed to be given to the maintenance and securing of markets I would like an answer to the question: If that is so, then how is it that the coal mining industry in my constituency -and I expect this applies to others-is working practically half time, two and one-half days a week?
Now, Mr. Chairman, I recognize that over the years there has been some considerable assistance given to the coal mining industry by way of subsidizing the movement of coal, sums of money which were given of course to the railways in order that they might bring down their freight charges on coal and therefore find markets some distance from the coal mining areas. I would like to point out, although perhaps it is not too strong a point, that according to the estimates about $6 million is being appropriated this year for the movement of coal and I believe there is a further supplementary estimate of another $2 or $3 million-I have forgotten just how much. We appreciate that but I would point out that the gold mining industry, which keeps nobody warm, which turns no turbines, which fuels no trains or ships, and which is of no value whatever except for plugging your teeth, or making a watch chain or

wedding ring or something like that, has been given about $11 million in direct assistance-as a pure gift.
Now, we have been hammering at this business for a good many years since we came into this house. Last year the hon. member for Red Deer gave a speech on this same thing, deploring the fact that in all these years we have not arrived at a satisfactory national policy for coal. The hon. member for Bow River time and time again has risen in this house with the same plea. So has the hon. member for Lethbridge, who has a large coal mining industry in and around the city of Lethbridge. There are others who represent constituencies where there are coal mines, and we have been hammering at this for years. I would like to know from someone on the government side of the house, and perhaps the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys can answer, why it is that we have a national policy for everything under the sun except coal. We have a national agriculture policy; we have our Canadian wheat board, the channel through which all wheat in Canada is sold to the world; we have a cattle policy; we have the Agricultural Prices Support Act, a policy written right into the laws of this country; we have a railway policy; and we have a radio policy. Those are all governed by the law. We have a trade policy geared to meet particular trade situations; we have an immigration policy; we have a veterans affairs policy; we have an external affairs policy which is geared to meet various world movements, things that happen on the world stage in this day of change. However, when it comes to a coal mining policy, in a country with such vast coal resources which can be changed into all sorts of other types of production, which can drive our engines, drive our industries and create power, electricity and steam, what have we?

I think that I have said nearly enough on this item, except that I must say this additional word. A few years ago the government set up an admirable commission to study this whole coal mining industry from coast to coast, markets and types of coal. I believe that commission made one of the best reports we have ever had during the history of this country. Judge Carroll at the time headed that commission, and he now has the distinction of sitting in this House of Commons. The Carroll coal commission came up not only with a report that was admirable but with certain recommendations. I doubt very much whether any of those recommendations have ever been put into effect.
I am going to suggest to the minister that a small commission-it does not have to be a commission but perhaps a select body-should be chosen to go through the report of the Carroll commission. Then, the government could take action to put those recommendations into effect.
We have a rather peculiar situation in respect to the coal mining industry today. I intend to be quite brief at this trying stage of the session, Mr. Chairman, but I wish to make a few observations on this first item. The minister's department carries on a great deal of most interesting work, and work of great value to the country as a whole. In my opinion there are not many members of this house who have a full knowledge of the work carried on by the minister's department, and I am quite sure that work is almost unknown to large numbers of Canadians. It is the opinion of this group that in the coming session it would be wise for the minister to have his estimates go before the committee on mines, forests and waters, so that the members of the house who are on that committee will have an opportunity of hearing the heads of the various branches, thus gaining a fuller understanding and appreciation of the excellent work undertaken by the minister's officials.
I rise particularly at this time, Mr. Chairman, to bring to the attention of the house the concern of large numbers of miners and the operators of small base metal mines in my constituency who have written to me about the closing down of certain mines and the consequent increasing unemployment of miners in the district I have the honour to represent. As the minister knows, that is mainly occasioned by a drop in the price of base metals, and to some extent by the increase in smelting costs charged by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. I have an extract here from the Nelson Daily News, dated April 23, 1953, which is headed: "Six Kootenay mines close in last year; prices blamed."
Everyone knows that owing to the rise in the price of base metals after the commencement of the Korean war, there were some properties developed and operated which, at the present time, it is strictly uneconomical to operate. These properties simply have to suffer the consequences of a decline in prices, but there are other properties that are not of that character which find themselves in difficulty now. I know that, in the first instance, this matter is the responsibility of the government of British Columbia; we recognize that fact. But I do suggest that this situation requires co-operation. The minister should visit British Columbia, if at all possible, and meet the minister of mines in


British Columbia to discuss what could be done. They together should meet the representatives of the miners and the major mining companies to see what could be done as a result of government and industry cooperation to meet this developing situation, which is so serious to quite a number of my constituents. I urge the minister to give every consideration to making a trip to British Columbia to meet the minister of mines and advance the federal government's position and learn the provincial government's position.
Secondly, Mr. Chairman, I believe that a large corporation like Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company should accept some responsibility for assisting these smaller operators. This company should meet the smaller operators in co-operation with the provincial minister to ascertain if it is possible to continue some of these marginal operations. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company has a monopoly on smelting by virtue of its tremendous investment in plant, beyond the resources of small operators. Without any question its operations have brought great prosperity to the part of the country I have the honour to represent. It is not possible for the smaller operators to erect a smelting plant of that size, or to get the value from the ores this company gets because of its experience, knowledge and huge investment. Then again, this company has almost a complete monopoly of power resources in the south Kootenay country. I think in that connection the company has a responsibility to the smaller operators and to the people of this country.
In addition to that, Consolidated Mining and Smelting has almost a complete monopoly of the raw materials, with a large mountain of zinc and lead ore at Kimberley and another large mountain of ore in the Arrow lakes in reserve which has recently come into the possession of that corporation. On those accounts I think a company of this size has a responsibility to the industry as a whole, to the smaller operators and to the people. I suggest to the minister that if he has an opportunity to discuss this question with the provincial minister of mines, that fact should be brought to the attention of the company, and that they have a duty to do all they can reasonably be expected to do, to assist these mines that will not be able to operate if they are charged the present smelting prices. 1 believe that if the management of the company had this situation brought directly to their attention by federal and provincial governments they would be willing

to co-operate and do something, to keep the economic base metal mines in the Kootenays operating at the present time. The hon. member for Kootenay East spoke on this question when we were going into supply some two weeks ago. I quite understand his concern because, like me, he represents a constituency which includes a large number of miners and some people operating small base metal mines. After he discussed the situation in this house he placed on the order paper a resolution which is in the following terms:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of introducing legislation for the imposition of substantial export duties on nickel and asbestos being exported to the United States during periods in which that country imposes excessive import duties on lead and zinc.
Mr. Chairman, we quite appreciate that circumstances may develop which would require urgent and drastic measures as suggested by this resolution. But we in this group believe in doing everything we can to develop freer trade throughout the world; and we hope that, as a result of the visit of the Prime Minister to Washington, such a course of action as that suggested by the hon. member will not be necessary. Quite recently we adopted unanimously in the house a resolution which demonstrated that the Prime Minister went to Washington with the full support of every party and of all members in the house, to urge on the government of the United States that they reconsider some of the restrictive trade policies that have been mentioned in the papers and dispatches and give consideration to Canadian needs and Canadian requirements as a good neighbour, not as a hard-shelled, ruthless competitor. I am hopeful that, as a result of the Prime Minister's visit, the United States government will not permit the increase of import duties as suggested a week or two weeks ago and that we shall be able to negotiate a trade policy on this and other matters that affect the province from which I come so that there will be some improvement in the present situation, and unemployed miners return to work.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I again suggest to the minister that, in a situation like this, everything be done to co-operate as closely as possible with the minister of mines in the provincial government of British Columbia, whoever he is.

I now want to turn my attention to the coal problem because it is an extremely important one not only in the province from which I come but in Canada as a whole. It seems to me that we should be taking a greater interest in the development of our coal industry, not merely from the selfish point of view of those of us who live in coal-mining areas but because it is, as a matter of fact, a national problem. Coal mining is something which, in my judgment, is extremely important in the economy of the nation. We recall quite well that during the last war we ran into some difficulty in supplying coal to the markets of Canada. It will be recalled that the United States found, almost overnight, that they needed a great supply of coal and that they could not continue to ship to Canada the amount of coal they had been shipping there previously. We were thus thrown on our own resources. Mining is that type of industry which just cannot be revived overnight. If we are so unfortunate as to be again involved in a war, it is likely that we shall find ourselves in the same condition as that in which we found ourselves the last time, and that we shall suddenly have to appeal to the industry in this country to revitalize their efforts in producing coal. You cannot produce miners overnight. In most cases mining is a lifetime occupation and those who are employed in that type of work come from people who have been so employed from generation to generation.
I spoke on this question earlier in the session and I have spoken on it almost every session since I have been in the House of Commons. On this occasion I do not want to repeat what I have said in the past. I know that we are getting close to the prorogation of parliament, and we do not want to prolong the discussion too long. Nevertheless, there are some things that I think I must indicate to the minister.
I have here before me a couple of newspaper clippings from Calgary, one from the Calgary Herald and one from the Albertan, which give a good picture of the way in which our mines are fast closing, and the way in which the industry is being closed out. I do not want to read them, but let me just put on the record some of the statistics which
