I do not think it should receive any subsidy. I am glad the minister has cleared up that point because it did appear to be so from this article that appeared in the Albertan of April 17, 1953.
We should look at this problem of subsidies from the broader point of view. Some people seem to criticize the paying of subsidies. I am not one of those. I can understand that we could soon get into a position where we would be subsidizing everything. I say, I am not one of those who criticize subsidies where they are drastically needed. We are giving assistance to various industries in this country in one form or another. There is hardly a major industry in Canada that does not get protection in some form or other, probably in the form of tariff protection as is true of radio and television sets. You cannot bring a television set in from the United States without paying 15 per cent excise and 10 per cent sales taxes. That is a very decided form of protection. In fact, it is a subsidy. Our television sets sell for a good deal more in Canada than do the same types of television sets in the United States. The same thing is true of the automobile and other industries. I am not picking those two out in order to criticize them; I just want to point out that we are assisting other industries in one form or another. When someone objects to subsidizing industry, in my opinion he is not on very good ground.
The hon. member for Macleod referred to the gold mining industry. We are subsidizing that industry to the extent of about $10 million to $11 million a year. The total for the last four years has been $40 million, and with this year it will be over $50 million. With a yearly production of about $100 million, that means a subsidy of about 10 per cent, which is a rather good one.
It seems to me that if we can go to that extent in subsidizing the gold mining industry -I am not criticizing that action at the moment although there is room for criticism- an industry that employs only 23,000 people when there are thousands of people employed in the coal mining industry, there is indicated a great need for an increase in the amount of the subvention in order that these coal mines may be kept alive. We will need these mines in time of emergency and we dare not allow them to be closed down.
The situation in the coal mining industry is extremely bad and unless the government takes the action which it has the power to take through the coal board this industry is indeed going to be in bad straits before very long. Men are being laid off and coal mines are


closing up according to the return from which I quoted a moment ago. In the Drumheller valley, in the Crowsnest pass and in the maritimes you find miners working only two or three days a week. How is a man going to make a living on that?
Some people point out that high wages are being paid to coal miners, that in some instances a coal miner may get $10, $12 or $13 a day, and it is contended that that is exorbitant. But when you find out that that may be the total amount he gets for a whole week's work, it does not look very good. The economic condition of miners in the Drumheller valley and other places in Alberta and throughout Canada is getting to be such that they cannot make a living. The stores in these localities are having to finance these men over the summer in the hope that in the winter there will be more coal orders and they will be able to pay their grocery bills. As the hon. member for Macleod pointed out, these conditions are quite similar to those that existed in the hungry thirties and yet we are supposed to be in a period of our greatest prosperity.
It seems to me that if we can adopt a national policy in connection with other types of production, we can do the same thing for coal. On April 23 the Minister of Trade and Commerce was reported on page 4307 of Hansard as saying:
We will continue to sell Newfoundland fish just as we have sold it ever since Newfoundland became part of Canada.
That indicates that something is being done for the fishing industry. It has been pointed out that the government is doing something for the agricultural industry. I am not criticizing that for a moment, but I do submit that government policy today is not such that it will keep this most important industry of coal mining even alive. Under present conditions the mines are going bankrupt and are closing down and miners are being thrown out of work.
Just the other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated clearly that he was putting in a national fuel policy in connection with gas and oil. But that is something that affects Ontario and Quebec. It seems to me that when anything affects Ontario or Quebec something is done about it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that there would be no export of gas until Ontario's needs were supplied. I am not criticizing that, because I think Canada should come first; but if we can do that for gas and oil, why cannot we do it for coal?
The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys has said that Ontario is a good market

for coal; the Minister of Trade and Commerce says that Ontario and Quebec are a good market for gas, the difference is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is going to do something about it; he is not going to permit any more gas to be shipped out until Ontario and Quebec are supplied. I submit that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys should make a similar statement and say that we are not going to have any more coal come in here from the United States to bankrupt our coal mining industry; we are going to keep Canada as a Canadian market.
If we can do it for gold, if we can do it for gas and oil, if we can do it for fish, if we can do it for agriculture, surely we can do it for the coal mining industry. This industry is essential, not only in times of peace but urgently so in times of war. I do not want to carry on the debate any longer, but I do contend that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys should make a greater effort. 1 was going to say that he should copy the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I do not suppose he needs to do that. On the other hand, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made some drastic statements in regard to the marketing of fish and the marketing Qf gas and oil, and I think it would be quite in order for the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to say to him: "You are doing that for Canada in those respects, we are going to do something for coal." If he would io that I can assure him that he would have full support from this side of the house.

On Wednesday, December 3, I placed a question on the order paper regarding uranium deposits in the county of Haliburton. My question was as follows:
1.	Has the government of Canada or any department thereof been asked to permit the exportation to the United States of any uranium ore or concentrates?
2.	If so, by whom?
3.	Has uranium ore from the area in or around the county of Haliburton in Ontario been delivered to any department of the dominion government in Ottawa for research and assay?
4.	If so, by whom was such uranium ore delivered?
5.	What was the result of the researches made or assays taken, and was any report made to the party or parties making such ore deliveries?
6.	If not, for what reason?
At that time those questions were wiped off the order paper, just as quick as the snap of a finger, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He said that the information required was of a secret nature, and that it was not good for the public to know anything about this sort of thing. Well, the only secret part of that development in Haliburton has been the secrecy of the government in blocking it since 1930.
I have here a book written by Hugh K. Spence and R. K. Carnochan back in 1930. One of those men was a top man in the minister's department, and they -have been convinced of the importance of this deposit for the last fifteen years. Yet the people
5282	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys up there cannot obtain an assay report. I would like to know why.
After sending samples to the department the people were told that the sample had been hand-picked. Well, if the minister or anyone else in his department can tell me how you can hand-pick 20 tons of uranium ore to send down here in trucks, I would like to know how it could be done. How could one hand-pick chunks weighing 300 pounds each? I say that this was a fair sample, picked out by shovel. It was not taken from one small section of the area. When the sample was taken four shovelfuls were thrown out and one thrown on the truck, and I say that would be a fair sample. Then the whole thing was sent here to Ottawa.
If there is nothing valuable there, why does not the department tell us so? Why is there all this secrecy? That is what we want to know. Why is the department blocking this development, from stem to gudgeon, all along the line? Why has it been doing so for the last twenty years? There is no doubt about it that Ottawa is not the only place from which one can secure an assay report. Ore has been taken in other places, and I do not mind that. But reports have been made with respect to it.
From the reports made by the best geologists on the North American continent it is clear that we have plenty of rich ore, a great big body of it. The government has spent large sums of money in northwestern Canada, and they are making wide searches for rich ore. Yet there is plenty of it, rich uranium ore, right at the back door of the Chalk River plant and the government does not seem to want to do anything about it.
I do not know why this question is considered so secret, because there is nothing secret about it. Everyone knows there is plenty of uranium ore in the Haliburton area; everyone knows it from Ottawa to Haliburton and right down through the United States. This government needs it, too; if they do not, or. if they do not know it is there, then why do they say that it.is so secret? Why do they not want anybody else to know about it, or to have anything done about it?
It is about time the department stopped trying to block the development of this important industry in Canada. On the other hand, it should be giving all the help it can. This is a most valuable product, something that is for the welfare of Canada, and especially in matters of defence. Indeed, it can be used for the defence of the whole commonwealth.
Perhaps the minister would be prepared to answer when he reaches item 216, if he is not in a position to answer at the moment.

speechtext:
My hon. friend's suggestions were largely to the effect that this government was not doing anything. However, I have a statement here which I should like to put on the record. I think it contains some very good suggestions and will answer a great many of the questions that have been asked this afternoon.
The development and application of a national policy for coal has been the subject of discussion and review by parliament practically since confederation. From the select committee of this house in 1877 to the report of the royal commission on coal in 1946, there has been a succession of investigations by committees of this house or of the other place.
The report of the royal commission on coal of 1946 is the last and most comprehensive of this series and, on the basis of the facts


produced, makes certain fairly definite recommendations.
The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking in this house on June 17, 1947, on the second reading of the Dominion Coal Board Act, reviewed the problems of the Canadian coal industry, the findings of the commission and the proposed action of government in response to those findings. The dominion coal board was set up as the first step in developing the policies recommended by the commission and direction and funds have been provided to the board since then for the further development and administration of these policies.
It may be as well to point out that the royal commission recognized that central Canada would have to continue to rely upon coal imported from the United States. The commission reported that the policy of assistance to Canadian coal mines through duty on imported coal and transportation subventions on Canadian coal was well conceived and administered. It was their recommendation that this policy should be continued at about the same level of assistance. It was stated that, in any application of the policy, due regard should be maintained as to the cost of the coal. ___________
The dominion coal board was created by legislation and brought into being by proclamation on October 21, 1947. The board at an early stage in its deliberations adopted, with the concurrence of the minister, a series of principles that in effect may be recognized as a coal policy. These principles are:
(1)	The maintenance of an adequate supply of coal for our national requirements;
(2)	The support of a sound and healthy coal producing industry in Canada;
(3)	The development of steady and adequate markets for the output from Canadian mines;
(4)	The provision at fair wages of reasonably full employment for Canadian miners;
(5)	The possible extensions of the market
for Canadian coals, with the resultant savings of foreign exchange.

 

..This may well be the proper time to see
how these responsibilities have been discharged.
The first principle is the maintenance of an adequate supply of coal for our national requirements. It has been proven by the circumstances of two wars, and buttressed by the report of the royal commission, that we must continue to depend upon our neighbours for a large proportion of our coal supply. The board in the application of this principle must consider, first, the national interest in an adequate supply of coal and, secondly, the local interests of the Canadian producers.

It is unfortunate that in this matter, as in so many others affecting our Canadian life, distance and transportation are stubborn factors that cannot be forgotten or refuted. A survey of the six years since the board was instituted in 1947 shows that over that period Canadian consumers of coal have continued to enjoy an adequate supply at all times. This is so, largely owing to the clear thinking and well founded practices of the larger coal consumers and suppliers who have built up a program of supply and stockpiling that has proved adequate under all conditions. The one possible exception to this record of success occurred through neglect of the long established practice of supply and stockpiling.
The second principle established by the board was the support of a sound and healthy coal producing industry in Canada. In 1947 the coal mining industry in Canada showed a profit of one cent per ton of marketable coal produced, and the over-all production was 15,869,000 tons. In 1951 the industry produced 18,587,000 tons and showed a profit of 36 cents per ton. It must be admitted that this past year has shown a drop in output to approximately 17,579,000 tons, but this is almost entirely due to natural conditions. It is a fact that the weather has been unusually mild, and this has substantially reduced the consumption of fuel. For example, the consumption by the railways fell off by almost one million tons. On first thought, this might be laid at the door of the diesel, but this is not correct. In 1952 there were certainly more diesels, but there were only some 46 less steam locomotives. These 46 locomotives might consume 130,000 tons of coal throughout the year, so that the remaining drop in consumption of 870,000 tons was due to either mild weather or falling traffic. A normal winter could easily build up consumption to the level of 1950 or higher.
The support of a healthy producing industry should not be construed as support for any one operation. All mining ventures are limited in time, and from the moment when the first coal moves out of any mine the exhaustion of the deposit forms a definite limit to the time of operation. Government support and assistance under our way of life should extend to the industry either on a national or an area basis only, and within that area of free enterprise should have full scope to maintain competition, to weed out the inefficient operators, to eliminate those mines where approaching exhaustion or other
13, 1953	5285
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys physical conditions preclude production of good quality coal at a reasonable cost, and to reward the efficient.
There is one segment of the industry that is noted in the royal commission report as requiring special attention, and that is in Nova Scotia. The situation in that most important part of our coal industry has not been as happy as elsewhere. This portion of the industry has received additional assistance recommended by the commission through the Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act. Through this means a large sum of money through loans has been made available for the modernization of the collieries. This program is at present under way, with the effect of some reduction in operating efficiency in the transition period, but with the promise of substantial improvement as it develops. It would appear from all the data available, as well as from the figures I have quoted, that the Canadian coal producing industry as a whole has been supported and has had a healthy development through these six years.
The third principle calls for the development of steady and adequate markets for the output from Canadian mines. Since we live in a democracy and believe in individual enterprise, there is a very definite limit to the powers by which the market may be attained. The policy of transportation subventions established in the early 1930's, and followed since then by successive governments, represents the means adopted. In 1947 there were 573,000 tons of Canadian coal moving to markets under subvention at a cost of $693,888 or $1.21 per ton. In 1952, the movement was 2,713,000 tons, and the cost $6,530,103 or $2.41 per ton. This is evidence of the application of this principle and the cost of that application. In our efforts to promote the establishment of these markets, we have gone farther than was recommended by the commission.
The fourth principle calls for the provision at fair wages of reasonably full employment for Canadian miners. I have a table here setting out the salient facts from which I shall quote. With the approval of the house, I should like to submit the complete table for inclusion in Hansard.

The wages paid in coal mining are among the highest in Canadian industry. In 1945, the average weekly wage as at December 1 was $39.72, while in 1952 it was $62.84 for the corresponding period. As a comparison, the average weekly wage for all manufacturers in Canada on December 1, 1952, was $56.05. During this period there has been a small drop in the total number of men employed from 22,227 in 1947 to 21,808 in 1952. This is due to increasing mechanization with the decreasing demand for hand labour. It is clear that the policies followed have resulted in reasonably full employment at fair wages for Canadian miners. I recognize that today's problems are slightly different from what they were in 1952. I am not saying that there is no trouble anywhere; I am just citing these figures as facts.
Finally, principle No. 5 mentions the possible extensions of the market for Canadian coals with resultant savings in foreign exchange. Since this was adopted in 1947, there has been a radical change in the exchange situation. This has not meant that efforts to extend the markets for Canadian coals have been neglected. The board is continually studying the possibilities of increasing our local markets and developing an export trade. The development of oil and gas in western Canada has had a great effect. Through salesmanship, work and government assistance the coal industry has managed to grow throughout the six years, but it must be admitted that the last two or three have been tough. The possible further extension depends largely upon increasing efficiency of
13, 1953	5287
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys production and lowering costs. The board will continue to work at this problem. This problem of increasing costs must be shared by both management and labour. It is possible that if Canadian costs continue to rise the product of the Canadian mines will be priced out of the market.
The industry in western Canada is greatly affected by the use and production of gas and oil. The hon. members from Alberta know that to be so. This affects the mines in the Drumheller valley especially, as they produce the coal which is good for domestic purposes but unfortunately does not store well enough to have a wide acceptance in eastern markets. In other words, it has to be used shortly after it is produced. This applies to many mines in Alberta. The industry, if it is to be expanded, has two main problems, in my opinion. The first is to produce a product of uniform high quality that will be worthy of consumer acceptance in competition with American coal. Second, it must produce a product that can be stockpiled. The reason I say this is that, in my opinion, if the Ontario market for western coal is to be expanded, there must be a reliable and continuing source of such coal available to supply the market when it is needed.
Enlarging on that point, I should just like to say that since I was given the responsibility for the coal board, in the fall of the year we have from dealers throughout Ontario very frantic appeals for western coal; usually when they need it worst, when they are supplying their customers for the first of the heating season, Alberta coal is not available.
Many types of western coal cannot be stockpiled and therefore are restricted largely to the local market.

I will enlarge on that point. In the past the practice has been to attempt to ship western coal to eastern markets during the fall and winter months only. Winter usually comes a week or two sooner in the west than in eastern Canada, thus creating a strong local demand which keeps the mines busy during the first few weeks of the heating season; and by the time the western market is supplied the eastern dealers have

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys begun to supply their customers from American sources. Further, the movement of western coal at that season of the year is always restricted because it coincides with the grain movement, with the inevitable shortage of transportation facilities.
In my opinion, the only way to build a stable year-round market for western coal in central Canada is by the establishment of marketing facilities whereby western coal of high quality could be stockpiled in strategic locations in eastern Canada ready for distribution when it is needed.
As I mentioned before, the province has the prime responsibility for developing its natural resources. They assumed that responsibility when these resources were given back to them. I am not criticizing the Alberta government at all. I believe that they are open to criticism just as much as is this government. They have collected large sums in royalties. I would urge them to spend some of the money that they are collecting, from the development of oil and gas, in helping the coal mining industry to develop a uniform product of high quality. That is one of the big obstacles that we find, or that the coal board finds, in promoting the sale of Alberta coal, namely the lack of uniformity in the product. I think the Alberta government could help materially in that one field especially.

I approached the previous mines minister and I mentioned it to Premier Manning the other day. He said that they had passed at the last session trade-mark legislation under which he hoped they could set up regulations that would help in this problem.
If this arrangement could be worked out by the industry-that is, production of a better product and the stockpiling in eastern Canada of coal capable of being stored- it would be possible to provide for year-round operation of the mines rather than seasonal operation, and it would provide a reliable source of fuel from Canadian sources for central Canada.
In conversation with responsible railway officials recently, I have been told that the railways would look with favour on year-round shipments of coal rather than seasonal shipments; and I am of opinion that this would be an excellent argument for the establishment of more favourable freight rates for the movement of coal.
The coal board will continue to assist the industry to help resolve this problem. I am not suggesting that the problems facing the coal industry are easy of solution. I know that the maritime coal industry is facing a very difficult period and will continue to have difficulties until the benefits from the mechanization program begin to show results.
I believe that in this review I have shown that the main principles, as laid down at the time of the establishment of the dominion coal board, which form the basis of our national coal policy, and as administered by the very efficient officers of the coal board over the last six years, have resulted in a period of stable operation, increasing employment and growing wages.
I am not overlooking the local problems. But in looking over the broad picture, I think one can say that the industry has not done too badly. We all hope that it can continue to expand and grow. As long as we believe in and live under a free enterprise system, the main responsibility for the solution of these problems rests with the industry. To that end I believe that the industry of western Canada-and I mention them because I know the operators better-are making an honest effort to help solve their own problems.
Hon. gentlemen have been suggesting that we should increase the subvention. I put that question up to the western operators association. I said: "Do you think that increased subventions are the answer to your problems?" They said, "No; we do not."

Mr. Chairman, I promised the minister when I spoke first that I was not going to speak any further. I am not going to speak at any extended length now because I know we are hoping to prorogue as soon as possible, but I did listen with interest to the minister's statement and I cannot help but feel that we have listened to the same type of statement for many years. His predecessors came up with the same explanation through the years. We have been sitting in this corner of the house for seventeen years now and have heard a similar statement made every year. The only difference between the minister's statement and the previous statements is the variation in some of the figures.
We have been told that the government is trying to create a sound coal mining industry, with markets and full employment. That has always been said and they are still working toward it. All because there is no overall Canadian coal policy. The minister mentioned those three elements in the government's attitude toward the industry. Surely the minister cannot say, when this large coal mining industry in Canada is working only two and a half days a week, that it is in a sound position, with markets and full employment.
If you read quickly the employment figures which he gave for 1952 they seem to present a more favourable picture than actually is the case. I can understand that those figures might be accurate for 1952. I have no way of disputing the figures and I suppose they are right. But if half the coal miners were working five days a week, if they averaged five days a week in 1952, and many others 68108-334
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys worked only two and a half days a week, then it looks to me as though some must have worked about eight days a week. That just does not add up. Perhaps in 1952 the Crows-nest pass area averaged more than two and a half days a week, but the point is that this is May, 1953. In May, 1953, the industry is working about two and a half days a week.
These coal miners have to pay rent just the same; they have to buy food just the same. It is small comfort to the thousands of men in a certain area who are working only two and a half days a week to be told that they should sit back and relax and be thankful because half the industry is working pretty nearly full time. That sort of thing would be a pretty slim fare.
The minister explained how the markets had become somewhat seasonal and that perhaps the coal mining industry had not been able to deliver coal at the proper time. All I can say about that is that it simply indicates the need for an adequate Canadian coal industry. This seasonal thing is not something that has happened recently. You cannot blame everything on the weather. We may have had a mild winter and that may have had some effect upon mines producing domestic coal, but the Crowsnest pass mines produce industrial coal. After all we have had springtime, summer and winter ever since the dawn of creation. To blame our difficulties on the seasons just indicates to me that we are in dire need of a coal policy.
I do not hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture getting up and saying that it is just too bad that they harvest wheat only in the fall, that it would be different if they would harvest it all the year round. They do not talk that way, because we have a wheat board and a wheat policy. Once again I say that there is need for a definite coal policy that will provide coal for the Canadian people, keep the industry solvent and bring about pretty well full-time employment.

Newfoundland is the only one of the provinces where the governments, either federal or provincial, actually operate the bait service. It was done by the commission of government and since confederation our federal Department of Fisheries has administered the operation. We took over the operation of the bait depots at that time. They are actually a losing proposition and we lose, on an average, about $170,000 a year. The bait depots are very useful as far as the fishermen are concerned and we agreed to take over those depots and operate them without fundamental change. One reason why the losses are increasing is that the type of fishing has changed. They are getting out of bait fishing and more into trawling and seining. Nevertheless there will be great need for these depots for years to come.
Another reason why they lose money is that, unlike bait depots run by industry in other provinces, they have just the single operation of freezing bait. In the maritime provinces these bait depots are associated with cold storage plants where fish is filleted and held. One of the recommendations of the Walsh committee was to try to develop plants around these bait depots which, as well as processing salt cod, would provide outlets for fresh and frozen fish. With that in mind the Newfoundland government approached the federal government and the suggestion was that we would turn back the bait depots to them. Under the amendment to the British North America Act we have the responsibility of seeing that bait service is maintained-but the provincial government in its proposal will obtain leases from those fishing operators in the province who will agree to take over the bait depots and extend them by putting in filleting machines and cold storage warehouses.
To us the proposition seemed a progressive one, providing that the depots were maintained. We entered into negotiations with the premier of Newfoundland on that ground. There has been a little misunderstanding in Newfoundland in one respect. It was thought that a crown corporation was going to be set up. That is not so. This offer is open to any one of the present industry operators in Newfoundland or to any other person who comes forward. The reason we have two

votes in these estimates is that until some agreement is reached which is acceptable to us, with our responsibility under the terms of union, we must continue to operate those bait depots. If during this summer or fall we can work out an agreement which will enable us to discharge our responsibility to the fishermen and at the same time enable these depots to be put on an economic basis and be used for something more than bait depots, we will go ahead with such an agreement.

speechtext:
This is the item which will permit the inauguration of this scheme of fishermen's insurance on boats and on one type of gear, which I referred to yesterday. In the house at various times comparisons have been made-not in a carping manner, but nevertheless there have been comparisons -between the facilities available to the farmers of Canada as compared with those available to the other primary producer of food, the fishermen. There is no doubt about it that fishing is an even more hazardous occupation than is farming. Because of the very nature of the industry, it has been more difficult for a fisherman to obtain definite aid in the form of either credits or grants or insurance.
That is especially true as far as the small fishermen's boats are concerned. The large boats-the seiners on the west coast and the trawlers and draggers on the east coast- are assessed and registered and can be insured by private insurance companies or by cooperative insurance companies at a reasonable rate; I think it is about 4| per cent. But unfortunately the great bulk of the fishing fleet, which is owned by the fishermen themselves or groups of fishermen, consists of boats which are smaller than that.
The private insurance companies have found it impossible to offer insurance to those classes of boats, for an obvious reason: The cost of administration would be so great in assessing the boat, and in having field men go out after storms, wrecks or fires in order to assess the damage. The rates quoted on small boats such as those I have mentioned would run from 12 to 20 per cent. Obviously no fisherman with a small boat can afford to pay such premium rates. Because of this situation the department this year made an investigation, as a consequence of the demand from every corner of the house from members representing fishing ridings that we should do something since the private insurance companies were unable to enter the field, and that the government had the responsibility to begin some system of vessel insurance.
The problem is limited first of all obviously by the value of the boats. We find that boats of a value of $7,500 could quite easily get commercial insurance. So the first step was to have our committee from both our

Supply-Fisheries
department and the insurance branch of the Department of Finance visit the coast and assess the storm damage. The hon. member for St. John's East some two or three weeks ago asked a question about the committee's work down in St. John's. They worked out what they thought would be an equitable rate for such insurance. We are now ready to go ahead with a provisional plan of such insurance.
That is one reason we are doing it by an item in the estimates rather than by legislation. It is a new field. It is a field in which we are going to have to gather a lot of experience. Hence for the first year or two we are starting with what might be called a rock-bottom plan in order to get the administration rolling and to gain with respect to such an insurance plan the experience which can be gained only by. having a plan in action.
The first approach was this. We quickly found that we could conquer this matter of costly administration because as a federal Department of Fisheries we have fishery inspectors, officers of our department, in every fishing area which is administered by the federal government. These men, with their regular duties, could easily combine the work of assessing boats and assessing the loss due to storm or other damage. That was a great step forward.
We then thought of confining the scheme for the first years to the coastal provinces where we have control of the fisheries, namely British Columbia, the three maritime provinces and Newfoundland. But various Quebec members-including the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine and also the hon. member for Gaspe in particular-protested strongly that this would be unfair on much the same grounds as those just mentioned by the hon. member for Selkirk, that the Quebec fishermen who were fishing in the gulf of St. Lawrence would feel that they were not getting the protection which has been afforded to other Canadians through the federal government. So we have now decided to have the scheme cover the five Atlantic provinces and British Columbia.
We propose to offer to the fisherman, by July 1 of this year, or as soon as the administrative details can be worked out, the opportunity to insure his boat and its fixed equip-ment-that is the engine-up to a maximum value of $7,500 for a premium of one per cent of the appraised value. In cases of total loss, there will be an indemnity of 60 per cent of the appraised value. In cases of serious damage-damage of over 30 per cent of the appraised value-there will be an indemnity of 85 per cent of the amount by which the 
repair bills are in excess of the 30 per cent minimum. We are having to include in this scheme the same deductible amount, to cover minor damage, as is common with automobile insurance.
To give an example, on a $1,000 boat- which is the common boat along parts of the Newfoundland coast and the maritime coast- the premium will be $10 a year. If this boat is lost or, if in the case of damage the repairs would cost more than the appraised value, the fisherman will receive 60 per cent or $600. In the case of partial damage, the fisherman himself must pay the first $300, which is deductible. In the case of damage amounting to say, $800, the fisherman would pay $375 and the indemnity fund would pay $425.
In addition to loss or damage to their boats, there is another factor of loss, and it is a significant factor. I refer to the loss of gear, traps and pots which are put out to sea and which can be lost by storm. Here again no commercial insurance is available. This is a much more difficult problem than that of boats, because of the expendable nature of much of this fishing gear and the obvious difficulties of trying to administer any form of insurance of this gear. We thought, however, that we should make a start on one type of gear in order to gain the experience which we will have to have before we can expand this scheme more widely; and we chose lobster pots as being the type of gear on which we should start this year. There are over 2 million lobster pots in operation in the Atlantic provinces. They are fairly costly, with the cost ranging from $3 to $7 or $8 a pot.
The losses through storms in recent years have been quite severe; the previous item referred to by the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth, for example, the item of $80,000 being our share of loans for losses of lobster pots in Nova Scotia in storms a couple of years ago. To make a start on gear insurance we propose to offer to the lobster fishermen, commencing with the opening of the fall season on August 10, in the Northumberland strait area the opportunity of securing partial coverage for lobster traps through the payment of a premium of $7.50 per one hundred traps for the legal fishing season. The premium will be $15 each for two seasons or a single six months' season. Some areas have only a single two months' season. There the premium rate will be $7.50 per hundred traps. In the area where they have two two-months' seasons or a six months' season the premium will be $15 per one hundred traps.
The normal annual wear and tear of course is a very difficult point when it comes to

insuring gear which is expended. Our committee examined the records and talked to the fishermen concerned, and it was generally agreed that there was a 25 per cent loss on lobster traps through wear and tear in each year. That would be the normal loss; and in order to take care of this normal annual wear and tear amounting to about 25 per cent of the traps used, the fishermen will have to take responsibility for the first 25 per cent of the traps which must be replaced in any given season, and it is on the abnormal loss that there will be an indemnity of $1.50 for each trap lost in excess of 25 per cent. For example, a fisherman with 200 traps will pay a premium of $15 for the regular two months' season, and he will receive $1.50 for each trap lost in excess of 50, which would be his normal wear and tear on 200 traps for a short season.
We would like to provide protection to fishermen using other types of gear, such as herring weirs, mackerel and salmon nets, cod traps, crab traps and so forth, but we feel that we must first gain experience in this field of gear insurance on the lobster traps. Our fisheries officers over this winter will be gathering data on the expendability of other types of gear so that perhaps next year we shall be in a position to extend this gear insurance to cover things other than lobster traps.
The other point of concern was the matter of credit for a fisherman who has lost his boat. A fisherman with a $1,000 boat, if it were lost, gets $600 back in insurance. He still has the problem of finding money to replace his $1,000 boat; he has to find another $400. In the four years I was with the Department of Finance I was especially impressed with the Farm Improvement Loans Act, one of the best acts on the statute books of this country, which has done so much for the farmer, in making credit available to him through the banks and has done so much for the farm implement industry in this country through the very greatly increased volume of sales-and it has not been a bad thing for the banks, either.
The banks have been unable up to now to extend such credit facilities to fishing boats, when the entire boat could be lost in a storm, and especially when it was so difficult to obtain insurance for the small boats. The large company boats and the boats operating as fishing fleets have been able to get bank credit, but the smaller fisherman has had to rely for credit on the local merchant or perhaps the processor to whom he sold his fish.
This committee made quite a study of the need for credit of fishermen in those areas,
Supply-Fisheries
and in contacts with the banking officials there was the feeling that if this insurance scheme does work out there will be an opportunity to begin a fishermen's loan improvement act somewhat similar to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, because the banks will then have some security for the boats that may be lost at sea. Therefore for this year we are not going to try to go into the credit field, but we shall see how this insurance scheme works out. If it works as well as we hope it will, we shall be in a position then to suggest some form of fishermen's credit parallel to the very excellent credit now available to the farmers of the country through the Farm Improvement Loans Act.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word about the companies branch. I shall not pretend that what I have to say is new, as the situation has been mentioned in the house on previous occasions.
This is a revenue-producing branch. The last annual report of the department does not indicate the exact revenue, but it is substantial. It is a branch that deals with the public and I think should be required to give service.
There have been certain changes in the branch. I think this companies branch has some very excellent senior officials in it. I cannot understand why it is that, when we look at the details as they are set out at page 478, we find provision for a salary of just $7,200 for the director of this branch. It seems to me that when you have a man of the competence of the present director, Mr. Cattanach, if you expect to hold such a man in this important position the salary range ought to be increased. It is very important, Mr. Chairman, that in a branch like this you have at the head a man whose competence is respected by those members of the legal profession who are dealing with the branch. I know that Mr. Cattanach does command the respect of the legal profession. And, looking at the salary range of $6,900 to $7,500 as indicated at page 478, it strikes me that that is not the kind of salary that is going to retain a man of his ability.
There is another point in relation to this matter which I think should be discussed. I have emphasized that this is a branch that is dealing with the public, and that the public is entitled to service. When a competent man is put in charge of a branch I suggest that some reasonable latitude should be allowed to him through the organization of his department, to give the kind of service the public

Supply-Secretary of State expects. There have been complaints for a long time from the legal profession about delays. This criticism is not directed against the senior officials of the branch, but the delays are laid at the door of the branch. It may be that there is not enough staff. It may be that the civil service commission, when they made their study of the branch, did not correctly apprehend the demands made upon it.
Nevertheless it seems to me that, to carry on the work assigned to it and to give the service the public expects of it, when the public is paying fees to the branch for the service it is to receive, a staff adequate to the demands should be provided; and the competent man placed at the head of the branch should have some reasonable measure of latitude in organizing it. The public looks to him to carry the responsibilities of that branch.

As this is the item for the patent office, we should, as has been customary from year to year, ask the minister if some progress cannot be made in reducing the backlog of pending patent applications. The last annual report, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1952, indicates the number of patent applications filed. We seek a reduction in the very large backlog which has been the besetting problem of this office for many years.
Again, this is an office that is set up to give service to the public, service for which the public pays. It is a revenue-producing branch; and I should like to say, as has been said annually for many years, that I think the present situation cannot be regarded as anything but unsatisfactory. Whatever progress has been made has not been enough to make a sufficient dent or impression in this heavy backlog, or to have come anywhere close to remedying the situation which has for a long time been highly unsatisfactory in a branch that should be giving prompt service to the public.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I realize that what my hon. friend has said is not altogether without justification. What he fails to take into account is the difficulties with which the department is faced. The work of the patent office is growing year by year, and it is not always easy to get staff to do the work. As a matter of fact, our staff is short at the present time. It is exceedingly difficult to get qualified examiners and, at times, equally difficult to hold them. The new applications received this year numbered 16,052. That is 604 more than we received last year. The number of cases allowed was 10,167, 44 more than last year. The number of examiners' reports was 12,282, 946 less than last year. The number of examiners' actions was 22,449, 902 less than last year. The number of cases disposed of was 13,644, 852 less than last year. The number of patents printed was 9,700. The number of patents issued was 184 more than for last year.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I thank the minister for
those figures which are, of course, more recent than those shown in the annual report of the department. However, I do not think
Supply-Secretary of State anyone can take any satisfaction out of those figures. I think they strengthen and underline what I was saying earlier; and, on the theme that the work of the department is increasing, let me make this observation. It is quite true that the number of patent applications in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953, as the minister has just indicated, represents an increase of some 600 over those for the fiscal year 1951-52. But, Mr. Chairman, the number of applications received even in this last fiscal year is not a record. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1947, we had 16,922 applications for patents. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1948, we had 16,585 applications. There was a substantial drop in the fiscal year 1948-49, but since that time the number of applications year by year has been rising steadily but slowly.
This department, Mr. Chairman, is not taking sufficient steps, it seems to me, to cope with the volume of work that is being placed upon the office. We can recognize that the present staff working under existing conditions may be doing its best; but the best that it is doing is not good enough to meet the needs and the proper demands of the public for service through the patent office.
This plea has been made year after year. We do not see any particular change year by year, and I think it is time the house made it quite clear to the minister that it is not satisfied with the way the department has been handling the problem. There must be something much more energetic, something much more far-reaching in the way of action to meet the volume of work and reduce this big backlog of applications, than is being done.
I do not intend to prolong my argument, Mr. Chairman, but I do wish something could be done to stir up the government to take action to provide what is required either in the way of staff or accommodation so the public may receive service commensurate with the need and with the payments which the public makes for services.

subtopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
It
may not be inappropriate at this time to make a brief statement of our financial position as we see it at the end of the fiscal year just terminated, and to comment on one or two items which might be of particular interest.
The estimated revenue for the fiscal year ending on March 31 will reach the highest figure in the history of the postal service. It will be in the neighbourhood of $130 million, an increase of approximately $8 million over the previous fiscal year. The estimated amount of revenues over expenditures will, however, be less than last year. This will be in the neighbourhood of $5 million compared to $6,500,000 for the fiscal
Supply-Post Office
year ending March 31, 1952. This is principally due to rising costs occasioned by such features as increased salaries for the employees, higher compensation to the railways, the extension of postal services to remote areas, and the development of better carrier delivery.
As an indication of the progressive trend during the last fiscal year, there has been an increase of approximately 8 per cent in the volume carried by rail. The number of ton miles of air conveyance has increased by 400,000 also 8 per cent. In urban centres the extensions in letter carrier delivery have brought service to over 50,000 additional families, while in rural areas rural mail delivery has been granted to over 14,000 new boxholders.
I mention these figures simply to indicate that we are still moving forward and at the same time endeavouring to live within our revenues. I think it is generally appreciated that it has been the policy through the years to give service within the limits of the revenues collected. This is a policy which is followed by a number of postal administrations, and I am sure you will agree that it is a sound one. It has been proven by experience, not only by our experience but by the unfortunate experience of others who have departed from this principle and as a result have incurred substantial deficits, which naturally impose an additional burden on the taxpayer.
This brings me to one item which I think I should mention, as it was referred to during my estimates last year; that is, the question of a return to the second delivery in the residential sections of the cities. I indicated last year that while we were not contemplating any change in the one-delivery system at that time, we did not entirely rule out the possibility of reinstating two deliveries when conditions were appropriate. I must say, with a certain amount of regret, that I do not feel that we are justified in incurring at the present time the added cost which the return to two deliveries a day would involve.
At the same time I must mention that we have been able to make substantial progress in the improvement of the service to the one-delivery area, either by a readjustment of routes or by other equally efficient methods, and I feel there is not the pressure for two deliveries which previously existed.
I might at this point refer to the steps which have been taken recently to improve the situation in regard to rural mail couriers. As you are aware, the house has given approval to a bill which will permit an adjustment in the contract rate to rural mail

Supply-Post Office
couriers. This it is estimated will add to our already mounting expenditures an increase of almost $1,500,000 a year. In addition there have also been pressing demands for increases in frequency and other concessions in regard to the application of the regulations governing rural mail delivery.
All these items are costly, but I feel sure I am expressing the desire of the majority of the members of this house when I say it is the general opinion that priority in the way of improvement in compensation should go to the rural mail couriers. Discussions which took place in the house when the bill was presented leave no doubt in my mind on that score.
Personally I feel it is my good fortune to be in office at a time when this measure for the improvement of the conditions under which rural mail couriers operate has been adopted. Not that I claim any particular credit for the benefits which will result, because I feel that members from all sides of the house have assisted in the passing of this measure. It is the result of a co-operative effort, irrespective of party.
I should therefore like to pay tribute to those members who sat on the committee dealing with the question of rural mail delivery. They did excellent work, and I wish to express my personal appreciation of the fair and impartial way in which it was undertaken. There was no evidence of partisanship, but simply an earnest desire to improve within reason the conditions of the rural mail couriers.
I should also like to thank the members of the committee for their words of commendation in regard to the complete information which was always available and to the co-operative and efficient manner in which the officers of the department assisted the committee in the completion of its task.
This is a brief statement I have to make at this time. I might add that I was asked a question by the hon. member for Peel about the conditions of the Brampton, Ontario, post office. I should like to make the following statement. The unsatisfactory postal accommodation has been known to this department since 1949, when an item for a new building was entered in our list of projects with the Department of Public Works.
A site at the corner of George and Main streets was suggested to the Department of Public Works but no action was taken because no funds were available. The category of the project for this new building has been raised to "A", top priority, on the 11th of April, 1953 and request made for early investigation of site so that it might not be

lost. On the 15th April, 1953, the deputy minister of the Department of Public Works stated "the real estate adviser will be called to investigate the site situation in Brampton." We cannot predict when a new building will be erected at Brampton, as no funds have been provided in the main or supplementary estimates of the Department of Public Works for this year. This is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works.

subtopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I just want to say a word
in connection with what the minister has said about not putting in the two mail deliveries a day, as we had before. The trouble with having only one delivery is that a district that used to be covered in the morning is sometimes not covered until the afternoon, because they took off postmen when the two deliveries were cut out and the postman now looks after one section in the morning and in the afternoon he will look after another district entirely. This has meant that people who are sending out business letters and one thing and another find that they do not reach their destination on time, although the mail might be in the post office. Because of the way deliveries are now made they are not delivered until the afternoon, and this has necessitated the use of special delivery stamps to ensure delivery of the mail in the morning. It has no doubt meant more revenue for the Post Office Department, but it is not good for business.
The minister said the estimated amount of revenue over expenditure is some $5 million. Is that net or gross?

subtopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: This is a paper surplus. We do not consider the cost of erecting buildings that are supplied by public works and the franking privileges which are given to members of parliament and others. It is only a paper surplus.

The post office took away
from the members some of the privileges they had. Members of parliament used to be able to register mail from here, passports and other things of that nature. Members of parliament now have to pay for that. I would think the revenue over expenditure would be a great deal over $5 million.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word at this time about the letter carriers who serve in various parts of this country. Earlier in the session we had a discussion on the rural mail carriers under a bill which was then before us, but very little has been said about the letter carriers in the urban centres. I think it would be well to recall that most of these men are veterans. As a matter of fact, for quite a long time it was impossible to get a job as a letter carrier unless you were a veteran. Many of these men suffer infirmities which may not prevent them from working in gainful employment but which may slow them up a little. That was all taken into consideration at the time these men were given jobs.
They are men of proved service and are employed in a branch of government which is possibly the closest to the people of this country. Practically everyone knows his postman by name. I realize that there are exceptions, but I think in most cases the postman is quite popular with the people on his route. The average postman has knowledge of their affairs. I recall during the war when the postman would be watching for letters from the boys overseas just as avidly as the people who were to receive them. They would watch for these letters as they sorted their mail, and their sympathies went out to the people who were eventually to receive them.
A mail carrier might say that Mrs. Smith down the street had received a letter from her boy, that he had just handed it to her. Soon everyone on the street knew that Mrs. Smith had received a letter from her boy. She would be getting telephone calls from people who wanted to know how the boy was, how he was getting along and so on. The letter carriers in these urban centres become part of the community; they are an institution.
I know you do get the odd character who may be a little rambunctious and who stirs people up, but that happens in any walk of life or in any occupation. You find people who are not properly adjusted, but I think by and large the letter carrier serves his community and serves it well. For this reason it gives me cause for anxiety to find out that relations between the letter carriers and the Post Office Department are not always the sweetest. I do not want to go into these in detail at this late hour and date, but I just want to say that I do not believe any controversy is always the fault of the one side.
Supply-Post Office
Where you have difficulties you generally find there are faults on both sides. Sometimes the fault is nothing more than a little belligerency, but it exists. If both sides indulge in that sort of thing you soon have a complicated and bitter situation. I believe that is what has happened in the relations between the Post Office Department and the letter carriers in various centres. I am not referring particularly to any one centre, but I do know that there has been difficulty in Hamilton and in Toronto.
I urge the Postmaster General to consider the situation that exists, and realize that these are men who have served their country well. Most of them are no longer young and, as I say, some have physical infirmities which, while they do not prohibit them from working, nevertheless slow them up a little. I think the minister should take that into consideration.
I should like also to refer to the salaries paid to these men. I think any man should be paid a wage which permits him to take his place in his community life on the same terms and with the same advantages that workers of comparable classes enjoy. So it was somewhat of a shock to me to learn that in the city of Hamilton one letter carrier applied for a house in the new housing scheme at the old airport which, I believe, is under the supervision of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This was a rental project. The man in question was earning $2,850 a year. He applied for a house in this district and was told that he did not make enough money to be considered a good economic risk, and that therefore he could not have a house in that particular district. The salary he was told would be the minimum was $2,964. Hon. members will see that there was a difference of only $114 a year between the amount he was receiving and the amount they said he would need to have before he could have a house. Nevertheless this man was prohibited from participating in that development.
Another man in the letter carrier service in Hamilton wanted to purchase a house under the National Housing Act. He was told that his salary was too small, that he was not considered a good risk by the mortgage company. He made $2,850, and the mortgage company said he would have to be making $3,000 a year before they would permit him to purchase a home.
It seems to me wrong that on the one hand the government lays down rules and regulations under which people can occupy certain premises coming under their jurisdiction, and on the other hand it prohibits its own employees from participating in those schemes which, supposedly, are for their enjoyment.

Supply-Post Office
The government proceeds to make rules which are detrimental to those people who make an effort to come under the scheme. Therefore I thought it my duty to draw these instances to the attention of the Postmaster General.
I am not suggesting that this matter of the occupancy of houses is one which comes entirely within the Post Office Department. Nevertheless I feel there should be some sort of co-operation between those departments which would permit people to participate in schemes which, actually, are the children of this government.
It is not my purpose to speak at greater length at this time in the session. If I have any further comments to make I shall make them when the respective items are called. I did think, however, that I should bring these points to the attention of the minister.

speechtext: Let me assure the hon. member that we feel the relations between letter carriers and the department are very cordial. At all times they are free to make their own representations to the officials of the department. So far as salaries are concerned, I can only say that we are ready to co-operate with them. But we must keep in mind the fact that, after all, this is a matter which comes under the jurisdiction of the civil service commission.

Perhaps the minister
would speak to his confreres to see if some scheme cannot be evolved whereby those people who operate lending institutions will be assured at least that a man who earns his living as a letter carrier is a good economic risk.

subtopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on this first item in the Post Office Department. There was a time in Canadian history when that was considered to be one of the most efficient departments of government in this country. I can remember when we could rely upon the post office as being exceptionally efficient. I think each time we have had a new postmaster general-and we have had lots of them in recent years-the service has deteriorated, and the relationship between the administration and the employees has also been deteriorating.
For instance, there was a time not so long ago when one could mail a letter here in the House of Commons post office on Monday afternoon with a reasonable hope that it would be delivered in Toronto some time on the following day. I find now, by actual experience, that if I want a letter delivered by Wednesday, or possibly Thursday, I must mail it here in the post office in this building on Monday. Last week letters I mailed here

on Monday were delivered in Toronto on Wednesday afternoon, and that was better than the average service.
That is one of the complaints I receive regarding the Post Office Department. I do not know what the trouble is, but I do suggest that two statements made this afternoon by the minister are somewhat revealing. He told us of all the extensions and improvements in the service. He made particular reference to extensions, and then he assured us that the department was still living within its revenue.
I do not know just what that means. I presume it means that this is one department of government where the economy axe has been applied. If it is, then probably the minister should be congratulated upon being the head of the one and only department of government of which that is true. And it is unfortunate that it should be true only of a department that is supported by the public, and should be pretty well self-supporting.
Another statement by the minister was that there is not now so much pressure for the two deliveries a day. This would indicate, I suppose, that the policy of the department is determined by the amount of pressure the public brings to bear upon it, and that so long as the public keep up that pressure they may expect some reasonable attention. But the moment they ease up on the pressure, then the department eases up in its service to the public. I suppose there is such a thing as getting used to certain conditions. I suppose one could even get used to hanging, if one were hanging long enough. The public, I suppose, does eventually become accustomed to the kind of inefficient service they get from this department, and gradually lessens its pressure.
I should like now to speak of employer-employee relations in so far as the Toronto post office employees are concerned, and particularly the letter carriers of Toronto and district. Toronto members will recall that nearly two years ago there was a joint meeting of the Toronto branches of the federated association of letter carriers and the Canadian postal employees' association in that city. I believe it was in the month of June. That meeting was held at the time the one delivery a day was first introduced, and there was a great deal of discontent expressed at the meeting. But all the discontent was not concerned with the disturbance which had been caused by the introduction of the one delivery a day.
That meeting presented the then postmaster general, Mr. Rinfret, with an eight-point brief. He assured the meeting that

since the points raised in the brief involved government policy he would present them to his colleagues in the cabinet for discussion and decision, and would let them know what decision the cabinet reached. Time went on from June until the end of October and no word had been received from the department as to whether or not these questions had been submitted to the cabinet. The association officials got in touch with the department, and about the end of November, or some time in November, the joint executive of those associations received a reply.
That reply was most unsatisfactory. Later in November they informed the minister of their dissatisfaction. That was in November of 1951, and I am told that not one word has been heard from the department regarding the eight points raised in that brief which the postmaster general of that time had given them every assurance would be discussed.
In the interval of nearly two years, as I understand it, one of the complaints that was raised has been fairly satisfactorily smoothed over and settled. That was the disagreement regarding the time allowed various letter carriers for their various routes. I understand that it has been settled to the satisfaction of the letter carriers.
I am going to remind the minister of some of the other points in the brief, since I have a copy of it here and since I am quite sure he is going to hear from those associations before long. They are seething with discontent at the present time, and I suggest that the Postmaster General give some consideration to the points which were raised two years ago and which I can assure him will be raised again within the very near future.
The first matter about which there is still some dissatisfaction is collective bargaining rights for postal employees. I know there is a section in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act-section 55, I think- which excludes civil servants from the benefits of that act. Notwithstanding that, civil servants and particularly postal employees feel that even within the limits of that act as it stands at the present time it should be possible for the government to give the postal employees certain conciliation and arbitration rights, which are enjoyed by employees of private industry. The letter carriers and the clerks in the minister's department in the Toronto area at least are very insistent that some steps be taken to provide them with some form of collective bargaining rights.
I know the answer that has been given by the minister and others on this question. I
Supply-Post Office
know the department considers that the national joint council of public servants of Canada is the body that has been provided, and that it should be competent to handle these collective bargaining agreements; but I am told by the representatives of the employees that the body is not considered to be by any means a satisfactory medium through which to carry on these negotiations.
In the first place, I am told, the role of the national joint council is specifically limited to that of an advisory body. While it was modelled on a similar organization in Great Britain it even falls short in some very vital respects, of that body which was in turn discarded in Great Britain some years ago as being unsatisfactory. Anyone who gives any study to this question, I think, must reach the conclusion that the federal government, and certainly the Post Office Department, is about the most antiquated, out of date, arbitrary and reactionary employer in this country. I believe you have to reach the conclusion that the government which supports private enterprise, which seeks to guide and direct private industry in its labour relationships, is itself far behind anything that can be found in private enterprise in this country.
The second point was that the employees asked to have a five-day week. I understand the government has taken the position that the five-day week will be granted when that can be done without any extra cost to the department. That again is not the position which the best employers of labour in this country take. The government again, instead of setting an example for employers of labour as it should, is itself far behind private enterprise, is itself creating or establishing anything but good relations with its employees in the matter of the five-day week.
The third point asked for at that time was an adequate cost of living bonus. I understand that at the present time postal employees are asking for an increase of $300 a year across the board. If one compares the salaries which are paid to postal clerks and letter carriers in the United States with those paid in Canada one cannot fail to see that the request of Canadian employees is very fair. I am told that in the United States clerks and letter carriers receive the same salary. The minimum for both in the United States, that is the starting salary for both, is $420 higher than the maximum salary paid to letter carriers in Canada. The figures I have are as follows. In the United States the starting point for both letter carriers and clerks is $3,270. Today the maximum for both in the United States is $4,307. I am

Supply-Post Office
told that the maximum-if these figures are not correct I want the minister to correct them-for clerks in Canada is $3,130. You will notice that is less than the starting point in the United States. The maximum for letter carriers in Canada is $2,850, as against the starting point of $3,270 in the United States, a difference of some $420. When one considers the salary that is being paid to clerks, which works out to $1.24 to $1.36 per hour, and when one compares those salaries with what is paid for similar work in the United States, I think one realizes that the request of the clerks and letter carriers is fair.
The next cause for discontent which I find registered by a number of correspondents on this subject is that when the department recently did give some increases in salary, those increases were granted only to those in specialized fields and those in the higher salaried categories, and were not granted to those who were doing the day to day work of clerk or letter carrier. Then again, if one compares the increases which private enterprise has given its employees since 1951 with the increases given by the post office to its employees, one is struck with the difference. According to the dominion bureau of statistics the increases received by the employees of private enterprise from December, 1951 to April, 1952 was 22 per cent. During that period the postal employees received an increase of 8 per cent. If one had the figures showing the increases in salaries paid by private corporations since that date one would find that the spread was still greater.
Those were among the points raised which caused the most dissatisfaction. I suppose probably the next in order was their request that they be given time and a half for overtime. I read in one of the reports that the officials of the department refused to consider the payment of overtime because of the nature of the letter carrier's work. It was claimed that the payment of overtime would only be an incentive to a slow-down. I wonder what we would think of any industry that took that position, that the payment of time and a half for overtime would only lead to a slow-down in production in that industry? That is the antiquated point of view the Post Office Department is taking toward its employees.
I think that, in the interests of good service to the Canadian people and in the interests of the morale of the employees of that department, it is high time the government brought its employee-employer relationships more in line with those of good employers in this country.

There were other points in this brief. The check-off was requested. I am reminded, of course, that before the 1930's the postal employees were paid time and a half for overtime. I understand that it was during the Conservative regime in the early thirties that the practice of paying time and a half for overtime was discontinued. Apparently the Liberals have thought it wise to follow one of the worst features of that particular Conservative regime. They are still carrying out the policy introduced by the Conservatives in the thirties.
I understand that it is close to 30 years since the postal employees' association was deprived of the right of the check-off. I do not know just what will be the effect of the new regulation which the government has announced regarding the check-off. I should like the Postmaster General to tell us whether or not the letter carriers who belong to an association that is affiliated with the Toronto labour council will enjoy the benefit of the check-off or if it will only be those who belong to the civil service association who will enjoy that right. I think the minister should clear up that point for us. Those are a few of the things I want the minister to explain.
There are one or two other matters I wish to mention. I have been asking in this house for about eight years now for a post office for York township. We have a municipality of something over 100,000 people. The only explanation I got from the department for their reluctance to give us a postal building is that a postal building in the township would not diminish to any great extent either the distance or the time occupied by letter carriers in travelling from the post office to their routes. In my opinion that should not be the criterion which should decide whether or not a municipality gets a postal building. There are many services that can be rendered to communities where there are regular postal buildings instead of a whole series of branch post offices tucked away in hardware stores, cigar stores and every other kind of store where there happens to be a good Liberal supporter.
I want to say this. Representing that riding as I do, in my time I have seen post offices taken away from businessmen who were giving reasonable service and given to others for no other reason in the world that I can discover except that they were good Liberal workers or good Liberal ward heelers.
I suggest to the minister that this is a public service and that the service which one renders, as a ward heeler of the Liberal

party, should not be a deciding factor in determining where that sub-post office should or should not be located. If we want to get certain information, or several types of service, we have to travel down to one of the city post offices. For the life of me I cannot see why a municipality of nearly 100,000 people in this day and age should not have a post office building in their township. It is a completely urban township. There is only one reason I know of, and that is that this particular riding has never elected a Liberal to this house. about Toronto postal station "Q", I should like to do so. The new building will provide greatly improved accommodation for postal patrons.
