Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal with two items in the estimates of the Department of Resources and Development. The first of these has to do with national parks and is connected with item No. 369 which, in terms of the total amount of the estimates, seems rather insignificant. This item deals with a grant in aid for the development of the international peace garden in Manitoba, and the amount set aside is $10,000.
My reason for making reference to this item is that, in the first instance, to the great distress of a large number of people who were interested in this project, it disappeared from the estimates last year. Then, secondly, it reappears this year at a reduced amount. The original amount was $15,000 and this year, as I have said, it is down to $10,000.
I should like to thank the minister for the attention he has given to this matter. While the amount seems small in comparison with larger sums set aside for other projects in his department, I assure him it means very much to those who are deeply interested in the development of the international peace garden on the border between the province of Manitoba and the state of North Dakota. It is significant that at this same time the House of Representatives in the United States is dealing with an appropriation for a similar purpose. A bill has been introduced in the United States house to provide for an amount of $100,000 which will assist in the development of the American side of this peace garden project. I would say at once that the target of $100,000 which, incidentally, is an appropriation to cover a period of three years, suggests that we in this Canadian House of Commons should consider restoring the grant in respect of the peace garden to its original amount of $15,000, or an even higher sum.
In terms of the value received from the grant, and the significance of the purpose of the peace garden, this is a very small amount indeed. Last year when the appropriation


was withdrawn I made some observations on the subject which I trust hon. members will recall. I shall not repeat those remarks in detail, other than to stress again the fact that this peace garden idea developed spontaneously back in the early thirties, and sprang first from the minds of people in the eastern part of the United States and Canada.
The whole purpose of the project was the preservation of peace. It was conceived to produce a meaningful symbol of the brotherhood of man. After a good deal of exploratory effort the committee in charge of the development of the project located, in what was thought originally to be a God-forsaken part of the country, a natural place of beauty straddling the Manitoba-North Dakota boundary. In 1932 a cairn made from native stone was erected formally initiating the garden. That cairn was inscribed with the following dedication pledge:
To God In His glory
"We two nations dedicate this garden and pledge ourselves that as long as men shall live, we will not take up arms against one another."
There is the emphasis of the peace garden, and I am sure members from all sides of this house will agree that it is a very worthy objective indeed. Last year the corporation and the committee-a voluntary board, I might say, which is largely responsible for sponsoring the garden-faced very difficult circumstances because of the withdrawal of the Canadian grant. They weathered the storm after considerable activity in raising funds in the local district.
From another standpoint the year just past has been an outstanding year for the garden. As a result of the publicity which arose from the withdrawal of the grant there has emerged on both sides of the boundary a new appreciation, a new awareness of the significance of the garden. For example, for the first time last fall, on October 1 to be exact, an international gathering of students was held at the site of the international peace garden, when students from Minot state teachers' college and Brandon college gathered to discuss international affairs. The importance of the gathering will be appreciated when I tell members of the house that the director of the Canadian institute of national affairs considered the gathering of sufficient importance to grace it with his presence. Dr. Edgar Mclnnis was the guest speaker on that occasion.
That was a new step forward in the realization in the purpose of the garden. This year, I understand, another interesting event is

going to take place. The federated women's institute of Canada is meeting in Toronto during the month of August. They are hosts to the countrywomen of the world, an international gathering of women's organizations. They are going to make a pilgrimage to the site of the international peace garden during their deliberations. That, I am sure, will suggest to hon. members that there is a growing appreciation of the symbolism and idealism that lie behind this very worthy project.
Most important, as a result of the publicity that has arisen, I feel certain that the minister himself, members of the government, and members from all sides of the house are now aware that this international peace garden is not a parochial or localized effort but has actually achieved what the description indicates it to be. It is a project, a development of international significance. I do extend an invitation to hon. members and to the minister in particular when he is out in that part of the country to pay a personal visit to the development. I think he will be quite impressed with what is taking place there. Perhaps he has already had the opportunity, I am not sure; but we certainly do extend that invitation.
This is a unique experiment, the only one of the kind in the world. It is North America's living message of good will located at just about the geographic centre of the North American continent. It is located on a highway that is destined to become an artery of tourist travel for the Americas. It is located on the highway that is a direct route to South America, and which will eventually carry right through to the port of Churchill as northern Manitoba is opened up. Becausfe of that it is going to become of increasing significance as a tourist artery.
Now for just a few minutes I wish to turn to the section of the estimates dealing with the Canadian government travel bureau. On this north to south highway, which is destined to become the tourist artery of the mid-continent region, we have perhaps the outstanding national park of all the national parks in the country, the Riding Mountain national park. Judging from its increasing popularity it is regarded as one of the major beauty spots in Canada. Everyone in the house is familiar with Banff, located in the Rocky mountain region. It is significant that Riding Mountain national park in a relatively obscure part of Canada draws the largest number of tourists next to Banff each year; and the trend has been ever onward and upward in recent years.
Supply-Resources and Development
Statistics show that the number of tourists visiting the Banff area in 1951 was 439,661. In 1952 the figure increased to 539,147, a total increase of 99,486. In 1951 Riding Mountain national park in the northern area of Manitoba had 334,059 visitors. In 1952 it had 389,163, an increase of 55,074. It should be noted that this was achieved with a minimum of publicity because, while Banff is internationally famous as a tourist centre, I am sure there are many areas in Canada and in the United States where people have not heard of the beauties of Riding Mountain national park. A radio commentator recently said that Riding Mountain national park is the most beautiful but the least publicized of all national parks in Canada. I believe the only booklet of the department which deals with Riding Mountain national park is the booklet called "Playgrounds of the prairies" dealing with all prairie national parks.
I understand that the department has recently initiated a radio program which is being very favourably received across the country, and it may be that they have given some special publicity to the Riding Mountain area. There does seem to be a need for a separate publication featuring this park which, with a minimum of publicity, has already attracted widespread attention and is recognized by those privileged to visit the area as being close to the outstanding if not the outstanding park in our Canadian national park series.
I think the Riding Mountain national park and the peace garden development are very closely interrelated. It is a part of this rapidly developing tourist artery which in the next decade or two will see thousands of American tourists-not only tourists from the United States but tourists from Mexico and South America-swarming into the central part of Canada to see the beauties of that area. I am sure the government is aware of this fact, because I notice in the estimates of the Department of Public Works an appropriation of some $160,000 which will eventually be used to construct a new customs port on the border to stand directly opposite the entrance to the international peace garden. This would indicate that in the very near future the government contemplates a great upsurge in tourist traffic, and is going to prepare for it by supplying adequate customs facilities.
I do not know whether or not the minister has ever thought of this next suggestion, but when we were discussing the national historic sites act, I thought if museums are going to be established at strategic places
533G	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development across Canada perhaps the site of the international peace garden might be the logical location for such a museum, in view of the large number of people who will be coming to that area.
So far as the preservation of relics of the early history of this country is concerned, Manitoba is relatively far behind. I know that in my own district of Brandon quite recently well preserved Indian burial grounds have been discovered with various cultural artifacts which belonged to the Indian dwellers of this country before the coming of the white man. These burial grounds are rich storehouses of the early history of this country. If these relics could be gathered into some central museum located in a strategic place in Manitoba, I am sure we would be able to preserve a record of the historic development of that part of Canada which, up to date, has had very little emphasis placed upon it and which because of neglect are rapidly becoming lost.
Those are the two matters that I wished to mention briefly. I need not prolong the discussion further, Mr. Chairman, except to re-emphasize that this main street of the Americas, as I am sure it will be called, will soon teem with tourist traffic. There will be a highway running from South America right up to port Churchill. With the mining developments taking place in the northern regions we are bound to have a highway development in that area shortly.
I venture to prophesy that this continuous north-south highway will become the main street of the Americas. My brief reference to some of the important places such a highway would serve has indicated, I trust, its growing importance. It would touch the international peace garden, the city of Brandon, the garden city of the west, Flin Flon, Lynn Lake and port Churchill, places which in themselves are fruitful sources of tourist attraction.
I suggest to the minister that the developments taking place in this area should be regarded as intimately interrelated and carefully nurtured. I am sure he will never regret the fact that the peace garden grant has been at least partly restored this year.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Edmonton East in his remarks early this evening discussed the route of the trans-Canada highway in western Canada. I thought perhaps he would expect me to make a brief reply to that. All hon. members know that the hon. member for Edmonton East has been a consistent advocate for many years of the route through Edmonton and thence down the Yellowhead pass.
The route of the trans-Canada highway, however, was chosen in the first instance by the provincial governments, subject only to the requirements of the definition that it shall conform to the shortest practical east-west route. The western provinces got together and, by themselves, decided that the trans-Canada highway route should go east-west through Regina, Calgary, the Kicking Horse pass, thence to Vancouver, thence to Nanaimo and terminate at Victoria. The total federal payment for this purpose amounted to $926,127.
Inventory work carried out by these provinces during the year included air photography covering nearly 107,000 square miles, field surveys in an area of 135,000 square miles, preparation of forest maps for 107,000 square miles, and inventory reports covering 46,000 square miles. Forest inventories under the agreements, which are to cover a gross area currently estimated at some 930,000 square miles, are now roughly half completed.
The federal government is also assisting in the reforestation of unoccupied crown lands by paying to the provinces $10 per thousand trees planted and $1 per acre seeded on such areas, provided the province's share of the program is not reduced below the average level of the past three years, and in addition the federal government pays one-fifth of the cost of establishing and operating new provincial forest nurseries. In the case of Prince Edward Island, where special conditions prevail, the federal government is sharing with the province, on an equal basis, the cost of a program for the reforestation of waste lands. In addition to Prince Edward Island, payments for reforestation in 1953-54 were made to Nova Scotia, Ontario, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan, the total amount being $102,109. Nearly 9J million trees were planted and two new nurseries were established in the provinces under the federal-provincial agreements during the year.

This year for the first time we have undertaken a series of radio programs through the Canadian government travel bureau built around the national parks and designed to stimulate in Canadians an appetite to see Canada. The matter I should like to raise particularly arises out of certain questions and answers which appear at page 820 of Hansard of December 17, 1952. These questions were put by the hon. member for Wentworth and relate to the construction of the head office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The questions and answers are as follows:
1.	What was the price paid for the land upon which the head office building of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is being erected?
Answer: An average of $824.30 per acre.
2.	What is the size of the property?
Answer: 281-5 acres.
3.	What acreage will be covered by the building?
Answer: The building and its grounds cover
21-3 acres.
4.	What will be the completed cost of the building?
Answer: The construction contract is not yet closed. Estimated completed cost is $2 million.
5.	What will the auditorium cost?
Answer: The auditorium is part of the general contract and is estimated to cost approximately $40,000.
6.	What will the dance floor in the auditorium cost?
Answer: The recreation floor is part of the general contract and the central section which is a spring floor is estimated to have cost about an additional $2,500 more than standard floor construction.
7.	What will be the completed cost of landscaping the grounds surrounding the building?
Answer: The landscaping is incomplete. The estimated completed cost, $35,000.
My concern is principally with questions 4, 5, 6 and 7. As to question 4, may I ask the minister if he is now in position to state the final cost of the construction? Second, what
Supply-Resources and Development was the cost of erecting the auditorium? Will he give the committee some of the specifications of the auditorium? Then I have a matter I should like to raise with respect to question No. 6, "What will the dance floor in the auditorium cost?" The answer to that question was designed astutely to avoid calling the floor a dance floor by referring to it as a recreation floor.

subtopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Turn handsprings on it, or what?

subtopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I think we can depend upon the minister to outline what other forms of recreation it is intended to carry out on the floor in question. I ask the minister to state clearly to this committee what additional cost was incurred in the construction of this floor. We are told in the answer to question 6 that it cost about an additional $2,500 more than standard floor construction because of the spring floor. I hope the minister will enlarge on that subject, because spring floors do not go with every form of recreation.
I think the minister knows my views on this subject. I do not think it is proper to use the funds of the taxpayers of Canada to build lavish structures. We know that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has a very important task assigned to it. It has become an exceedingly important government agency and has great responsibilities, and it is only proper that the corporation should be furnished with adequate accommodation. There are occasions when inadequate accommodation does give rise to inefficient operation and administration and in that way actually increases the cost of operation. But it seems to me that is a far cry from the sort of construction that has been revealed in the answers to these questions. *
